docs.title: v2 vs v3 on ROCm (same conditions)
docs.text:
The first row is the v2 baseline from the morning. In the afternoon both versions measured ~6% slower at c=1, so the v2/v3 comparison was re-run back to back: v2 code (commit 5910c31) and v3 each served from a fresh start, then clef bench --concurrency 1,4,8,16 --requests 100. v3 also ran 300-request c=1 runs: p50 148.0-150.3 ms, the same as v2's 149.1-149.3 ms in the same window.

conc v2 req/s v3 req/s (run 1 / run 2) v2 p50 ms v3 p50 ms 1 6.6 6.6 / 6.7 150.1 149.0 / 149.3 4 7.2 7.0 / 7.0 547.9 566.3 / 569.3 8 8.3 8.2 / 8.1 945.2 956.5 / 965.7 16 8.1 8.8 / 8.9 1766.5 1746.5 / 1754.3

Every level is within the 5% regression budget (worst: c=4, -2.8% throughput, +3.9% p50). The v2 c=16 run had a noisy tail (p95 2873 ms).

docs.title: Notes on the ROCm v2 run
docs.text:
• 100 requests per level; avg server batch 1.0 at c=1 and ~7.8 at c=16. Concurrency 8: 8.2 req/s.
  • Compute-bound: GEMMs ~83% of GPU kernel time at ~95 TFLOPS. Batching adds ~30% throughput, not more.
  • A ~330-token single forward is GPU-bound: kernel/wall 0.78 measured without the profiler (68.4 / 87.6 ms, 2026-10-18, MASK_FREE + FAST_HEAD + TunableOp). The earlier "about half is host overhead" came from wall time measured inside the profiler. With attention_mask=None the backbone captures into a HIP graph (transformers skips its mask check while capturing); replay saves ~27% at 64 tokens, ~5% at 128 and nothing at 384. Replay parity is not checked yet.
  • The joint head is ~5% of the forward. Padding to a multiple of 64 beat raw lengths and full buckets (CLEF_PAD_MULTIPLE); re-measure on other backends before assuming the same.
  • Warm restart: load ~45-100 s, warmup ~12 s with a warm Triton cache (~110 s the very first time).

docs.title: Quantization accuracy (CUDA only)
docs.text:
Measured on the RTX 4070 Ti (12 GB) against the lossless offload run (OFFLOAD=cpu CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB=10), not against plain bf16, because bf16 does not fit in 12 GB. Offload is documented to give identical probabilities to bf16 (0 / 0 on ROCm); that was not re-checked on CUDA.

Mode Max abs prob diff Mean abs diff Argmax agreement Latency vs reference int8, torchao (CLEF_QUANT_BACKEND=torchao) 0.066 0.0057 396 / 399 (99.2%) p50 170 ms vs 572 ms int8, bitsandbytes (CUDA default) 0.209 0.0172 377 / 399 (94.5%) p50 232 ms vs 572 ms nf4 (bitsandbytes) 0.444 0.0333 363 / 399 (91.0%) p50 153 ms vs 572 ms

The numbers match the ROCm run of the same two backends (torchao 0.0058 / 2 flips, bitsandbytes 0.0175 / 22 flips). nf4 also matches ROCm (0.0329 / 35 flips) and stays not recommended. Plain bf16 needs a 24 GB card and was not run.

docs.title: Smaller-memory options on ROCm (offload, int8, nf4), 2026-10-03
docs.text:
Setup: RX 7900 XTX 24 GB, ROCm 7.2, torch 2.11.0+rocm7.2, WSL2 (25 GB RAM), 2026-10-03, one configuration per process, bf16 measured first and last in the same session (152 / 154 ms p50, 4.72 / 4.67 req/s: 1% drift). Workload: 200 records (choice 2-6 options, score 3-5 levels, noul; 1-3 questions each; states of ~15-1500 tokens; 10 with an image). "single" = 100 text records one at a time through Engine.decide; "c=8" = 160 requests, 8 in flight, through the engine's micro-batching. Parity = every answer option's probability against the bf16 run of the same session, one record per forward (399 questions).

Setting Device GB, peak allocated / reserved Host RAM after load single p50 / p95 req/s c=8 Max / mean abs prob diff Top-1 flips bf16 (default) 18.4 / 19.4 1.5 GB 152 / 560 ms 4.72 reference - OFFLOAD=cpu cap 16 13.8 / 15.6 5.1 GB 169 / 600 ms 4.36 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 15 13.1 / 15.0 6.2 GB 175 / 597 ms 4.15 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 12 9.8 / 12.0 9.9 GB 327 / 648 ms 3.47 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 11 9.0 / 11.0 11.1 GB 343 / 634 ms 3.37 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 8 5.8 / 8.0 14.3 GB 498 / 667 ms 2.80 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 7 5.1 / 7.0 15.0 GB 540 / 671 ms 2.59 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 6 crashed (segfault while loading; 28 layers pinned on WSL2) QUANT=int8 (torchao) 12.0 / 12.9 1.5 GB 198 / 595 ms 4.23 0.062 / 0.0058 2 / 399 QUANT=int8 OFFLOAD=cpu (embeddings on host) 8.3 / 9.2 2.5 GB 206 / 611 ms 4.10 0.062 / 0.0058 2 / 399 QUANT=int8 QUANT_BACKEND=bnb (bitsandbytes) 11.6 / 12.7 2.5 GB 420 / 680 ms 3.01 0.262 / 0.0175 22 / 399 QUANT=nf4 (bitsandbytes) 8.5 / 9.2 1.5 GB 249 / 637 ms 3.66 0.449 / 0.0329 35 / 399 fp16 (noise floor, separate run, 200 text records) 18.2 / 18.4 159 ms (bf16 that run: 176) 0.021 / 0.0019 0 / 399
  • The cap is enforced on the PyTorch allocator. The whole process (reserved memory + driver context) measured about 0.65 GB above the cap, so use N - 0.5 GB for an N GB card: 15 for 16 GB, 11 for 12 GB, 7 for 8 GB.
  • Host RAM after load is the process RSS once the model is in place: the pinned copies of everything that was moved off the GPU. During loading RSS peaks higher (up to ~19 GB) because the safetensors files are memory-mapped; those pages are reclaimable page cache.
  • p95 is dominated by the longest records of the eval set (~1500 tokens), which are compute-bound and unaffected by the settings; p50 is the number that moves.
  • Offload latency is the PCIe copy of the streamed layers (about 0.43 GB per layer at ~26 GB/s) partly hidden behind compute; batching amortises it (req/s at c=8 falls less than single latency rises).
  • int8 flips: 2 of 399 questions changed their top option, against 0 for fp16 vs bf16. The mean probability error 0.006 is ~3x the fp16/bf16 noise floor.

Background: docs/memory.md. Reproduce with bench/memory_bench.py. CUDA and Apple Silicon rows are still pending hardware.

Mode c=1 req/s, p50 / p95 c=4 req/s, p50 c=8 req/s, p50 c=16 req/s, p50 / p95 int8 torchao + offload 6.2, 160 / 164 ms 8.7, 458 ms 8.7, 814 ms 8.7, 1830 / 2084 ms int8 bitsandbytes + offload 4.4, 228 / 259 ms 8.8, 428 ms 8.4, 968 ms 9.4, 1674 / 1897 ms

  • The lossless modes need more host RAM than a default 15 GB WSL2: OFFLOAD=cpu was refused at caps of 10 and 11 GB ("11.0 GB of weights stay in host memory, 13.0 GB free"), and the cap 10 run peaked at 17.1 GB of RSS while loading.

  • Not run: plain bf16 (needs 24 GB) and native Ubuntu.

docs.title: CLEF_PAD_MULTIPLE on CUDA (RTX 4070 Ti, int8 torchao + offload, 2026-10-12)
docs.text:
The default of 64 was chosen on ROCm. clef bench --requests 100 --concurrency 1,8, ~330-token records, a fresh server per run; the default (64) was measured twice and a multiple of 8 three times.

CLEF_PAD_MULTIPLE c=1 req/s, p50 c=8 req/s, p50 8 6.0, 165.5 / 166.5 / 166.1 ms 9.5, 880 / 866 / 869 ms 64 (default) 5.9, 169.3 / 168.9 ms 8.5, 942 / 949 ms 128 5.9, 169.6 ms 8.5, 956 ms

A multiple of 8 was about 12% faster at concurrency 8 and 2% faster at concurrency 1, consistently across the three runs. Only one mode and one record length were measured; the bf16 and mixed-length workloads are untested, so the default is unchanged.

docs.title: Speed flags and TunableOp on ROCm (RX 7900 XTX, 2026-10-18)
docs.text:
bench/perf_check.sh, one session, result cache off, fixed-length records (clef bench). Parity is against the flags-off engine (200 records, 10 with images; the flags-off engine run twice differs by 0.0, so the 2e-3 gate is the floor). Every top-1 change was a near coin-flip (reference top-2 margin 0.0015-0.017, the lowest 1.5% of the 399 questions).

Variant Parity: max |dp| / top-1 flips c=1 p50 / p95 ms c=1 req/s c=8 req/s c=16 req/s flags off (base) reference 133.8 / 683.7 4.5 8.5 9.1 CLEF_MASK_FREE=1 0.0235 / 1 137.5 / 610.0 4.5 8.6 9.0 CLEF_FAST_HEAD=1 0.0038 / 0 133.3 / 588.8 4.6 8.6 9.5 both 0.0235 / 1 133.8 / 585.6 4.6 8.7 9.5 CLEF_TUNABLEOP=1 (tuned) 0.0219 / 3 104.2 / 502.5 5.7 10.1 10.8 both + TunableOp (the ROCm default) 0.0273 / 0 98.6 / 452.3 6.0 11.3 11.8

Step 0 (profile_forward.py --batch 8): single record kernel/wall 0.22 with profiler overhead in the wall time (0.78 without it, see above), batch 8 0.68; GEMM 81-84% of kernel time. Accuracy on the 47 labelled tickets: 0.872 with TunableOp off and on.

Mixed-length traffic (clef bench --mixed), TunableOp off vs on: c=1 5.9 vs 7.6 req/s (p50/p95/max 151/241/249 vs 111/199/204 ms), c=8 6.0 vs 7.9, c=16 6.2 vs 7.9 (+27-32%).

TunableOp cost and design. On gfx1100 PyTorch already uses rocBLAS; TunableOp's gain is choosing better rocBLAS solutions (1054 of 1181 tuned GEMMs are rocBLAS, 66 hipBLASLt; tuned GEMMs ~40% faster than rocBLAS's own pick). Tuning costs a fixed ~4-8 s per GEMM whatever the per-candidate budget (30 ms / 100 runs, 5 ms / 20 and 1 ms / 3 pick equally fast kernels), so the ~535 GEMMs of the serving grid take about an hour. Tuning on the request instead (the old behaviour) gave single requests p50 2.7 s, p95 39 s until every shape had been seen. clef now tunes in the background while idle (a step only after 2 s without requests), never on a live request.

docs.title: vLLM vs clef (RX 7900 XTX, 2026-10-18)
docs.text:
bench/vllm/vllm_check.sh, vLLM nightly image vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-39983a5e… (clef-flash natively, max-num-seqs 8), 100 requests per level, same session. In-container ROCm on WSL needed ROCPROFILER_REGISTER_ENABLED=0 (the image's torch links rocprofiler-sdk, which is unsupported on WSL).

Line c=1 p50 / p95 ms, req/s c=8 req/s c=16 p50 / p95 ms, req/s c=32 req/s clef, flags off 137 / 145, 7.2 8.8 1748 / 1797, 9.0 9.0 clef, MASK_FREE + FAST_HEAD 134 / 138, 7.4 8.8 1663 / 1684, 9.6 9.5 clef, TunableOp 104 / 108, 9.5 10.9 1434 / 1443, 11.1 10.8 vLLM 136 / 157, 7.3 12.2 1304 / 1312, 12.2 12.1

Parity vLLM vs clef flags off: max |dp| 0.034, 1 flip (near tie). Decision on this card: not adopted (1.10x at c=16 against a 1.3x bar, 1.45x the p95 at c=1). Re-run the script on other GPUs before deciding there.

docs.title: Job feeding (length sort, tokenize ahead) and sharing the GPU (RX 7900 XTX, 2026-10-18)
docs.text:
bench/sort_check.sh (2000 long-tailed items x 3 for base and sort; quick run 600 x 2 for all four):

Variant Items/s Gain Labels Interactive p95 base 9.5-9.7 - - 734-805 ms CLEF_JOB_SORT_WINDOW=512 10.7-11.0 +13-14% 100% 786 (quick) / 926 (full) ms CLEF_TOKENIZE_AHEAD=1 9.5 +0.3% 100% 789 ms both 10.6 +12% 100% 1005 ms

Both stay off: the window's gain costs interactive latency. Interactive latency during a 3000-item job (unique requests, cache off): idle p50 140 ms; one job 622 ms (before the priority lane) vs 627 ms (with it); 2 keys x 2 jobs 624 ms, about one batch-8 forward.

docs.title: Hardware validation checklist
docs.text:
For maintainers with a real Mac (Apple Silicon) or NVIDIA machine. The unit tests mock the backends and never load the model, so they cannot prove these backends. Until this checklist has been run and its results pasted back, the README marks CUDA and MPS as "untested on hardware".

Time: ~30-60 min plus the ~19 GB download. Needs: 24 GB NVIDIA GPU or Mac with >= 32 GB (or a 16 GB NVIDIA for the quantized rows).

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
Follow the quick start for your platform in the README (lock file: requirements/cuda.txt or requirements/macos.txt), with the dev extras:

git clone https://github.com/MiguelCarrascoB/clef && cd clef
uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements/<cuda|macos>.txt
uv pip install -e ".[server,dev]"

docs.title: 2. Environment and weights
docs.text:
clef doctor --json > doctor.json     # keep this file
clef download                        # ~19 GB, resumable

doctor must report the expected backend (cuda or mps). On NVIDIA the "fast path is not available" warning should be gone once flash-linear-attention and causal-conv1d are installed; on Mac the torch fallback is expected.

docs.title: 3. Smoke test (loads the model)
docs.text:
clef doctor --smoke

Passes when one fixed record returns probabilities that sum to 1. Note the printed latency and load time.

docs.title: 4. Serve
docs.text:
clef serve --detach
clef status                          # backend, device, status=ready
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8910/health

docs.title: 5. Integration tests against the live server
docs.text:
pytest -m gpu tests/integration

Includes the check that /v1/classify matches the equivalent /v1/systemone call within 1e-3.

docs.title: 6. Benchmarks
docs.text:
clef bench --requests 100            # HTTP: concurrency 1/2/4/8/16
clef stop
python bench/parity.py               # dtype / quantization parity vs bf16 (needs the GPU, server stopped)

On a card too small for bf16, use the lossless offload run as the parity reference (--offload cpu --max-device-gb <N-2> --save-reference ...); the results table must say so. Smaller-memory modes (memory.md): run bench/memory_bench.py for bf16, --offload cpu --max-device-gb 15 (16 GB cards), --quant int8 --offload cpu (12 GB cards) and, on NVIDIA, --quant int8 --quant-backend bnb and --quant nf4 (pip install bitsandbytes). Save the bf16 run with --save-reference and pass it to the others with --reference (commands in memory.md), then paste the JSON results.

Optionally compare padding: CLEF_PAD_MULTIPLE=64 (default) vs 8 vs 128, since the best value was only measured on ROCm.

docs.title: 7. What to paste back
docs.text:
In an issue or PR (use the bug report template if something failed):

  • doctor.json (the clef doctor --json output)
  • the clef bench table
  • bench/parity.py output (max abs prob diff per mode)
  • peak memory (from /health or nvidia-smi / Activity Monitor) and load time
  • pass/fail of pytest -m gpu tests/integration, with the failing test output if any

Do not paste API keys.

docs.title: 8. Flip the status
docs.text:
When steps 2-6 pass:

  1. Add a row to docs/hardware-results.md with the numbers, device, date and clef version.
  2. In README.md, change the platform's support-matrix status from "untested on hardware" to "verified ()", e.g. "verified (RTX 4090)" or "verified (M3 Max, 64 GB)".
  3. Add a line to CHANGELOG.md under the next release.

    4. If something failed, do not flip the status; open an issue with the pasted output.

docs.title: Async jobs and webhooks
docs.text:
/v1/classify/batch holds one HTTP connection open until every record is done. That is fine for 64 rows and wrong for a 50 000-row CSV (~150 ms per record means about two hours). A job is the same work with the connection closed: submit it, get an id back immediately, then poll (or receive a webhook) and page or stream the results when it is done.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> queued: POST /v1/jobs (202)
    queued --> running: the scheduler admits it (class, fair share, window)
    running --> succeeded: all items processed
    running --> failed: systemic error, every item failed, or the circuit breaker tripped
    running --> cancelled: POST .../cancel (between chunks)
    queued --> cancelled: POST .../cancel
    running --> interrupted: server stopped / crashed
    interrupted --> running: server restarted, resumes after the last stored row
    interrupted --> failed: crashed more than CLEF_JOB_MAX_RESUMES times
    interrupted --> cancelled: a cancel requested before the stop / crash
    succeeded --> [*]: DELETE or retention TTL
    failed --> [*]
    cancelled --> [*]

Interactive requests (/v1/classify, /v1/systemone, ...) stay responsive while jobs run: up to CLEF_JOB_ACTIVE jobs advance in turns, but only one chunk (CLEF_MAX_MICROBATCH records, 8 by default) across all of them is in flight at the engine, and the engine queue has a priority lane: job chunks go in the background lane, requests in the interactive one, and the next micro-batch is interactive when any request is waiting (up to CLEF_INTERACTIVE_BURST interactive micro-batches in a row, then one background group). A request arriving mid-job therefore waits only for the job micro-batch already being computed (it is never preempted): one forward when the chunk shares a length bucket, more when it spans several buckets or carries media (one forward per media record). Cancellation also takes effect between chunks.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
All under /v1, same API key rules as the rest. Errors are {detail, request_id}.

Method and path Purpose POST /v1/jobs Submit. 202 with the job and a Location header. Rate limited like inference. GET /v1/jobs?status=&kind=&limit=&offset= List, newest first (limit 1-200, default 50). GET /v1/jobs/{id} Status, progress, ETA, timings, error, result summary, webhook delivery status. GET /v1/jobs/{id}/results?offset=0&limit=100 One JSON page (limit up to 1000). Follow next_offset until it is null. GET /v1/jobs/{id}/results?format=ndjson or csv Stream every row (offset / limit optional). Works while the job runs, but then it is partial: it holds the rows stored when the request arrived (the X-Clef-Job-Status header says which state that was). POST /v1/jobs/{id}/cancel Cancel a queued or running job (409 if already finished). Rows already produced are kept. POST /v1/jobs/{id}/webhook/redeliver?event= Retry a webhook delivery that ended failed (see Webhooks). event defaults to the job's own final event. Rate limited like submit. DELETE /v1/jobs/{id} Remove a finished job and its rows (409 while queued / running: cancel first).

docs.title: Submit
docs.text:
{
  "kind": "classify",
  "payload": {"inputs": ["Checkout is down", "Charged twice"], "labels": ["billing", "technical"]},
  "webhook": {"url": "https://hooks.example.com/clef", "secret": "s3cret", "events": ["job.succeeded", "job.failed"]},
  "metadata": {"batch": "2026-10-03"}
}

webhook and metadata are optional (metadata is any JSON up to 16 KB, echoed back on every read). Scheduling fields, all optional, are described in Scheduling: priority, urgent, schedule, expire_after_s.

Idempotency. Send an Idempotency-Key header (1-128 printable ASCII characters) and a resubmission with the same key by the same API key returns the job created the first time (202, plus Idempotent-Replay: true) instead of queueing a duplicate. Use it when the response to a submit may have been lost. The key is remembered as long as the job is (until it is deleted or purged); the payload of a replay is not compared. The Python clients take idempotency_key=, the JS client idempotencyKey.

The payload is validated completely at submit time: a mistake is a 400 with a path, for example payload.inputs: inputs must contain at least one item or payload.requests[12].questions: at least one question is required, and nothing is queued.

Built-in kinds:

kind payload Result rows classify inputs (up to CLEF_MAX_JOB_ITEMS), either labels or classifier (a saved classify classifier), optional instructions, multi_label, threshold, model {index, label, confidence, scores, input_tokens} (multi-label: labels, threshold instead of label, confidence) score inputs, either levels or classifier (a saved score classifier), optional instructions, model {index, score, level, level_index, confidence, distribution, input_tokens} systemone requests: a list of /v1/systemone bodies (media allowed, same per-request limits) {index, model, answers, input_tokens} evaluate the same body as POST /v1/evaluate (up to CLEF_MAX_JOB_EVAL_ROWS rows), see evaluation {index, input, gold, predicted, confidence, correct, scores}; the job result is the metrics object batch internal: created by POST /v1/batches (OpenAI Batch API); input_file_id, endpoint. A run where every line failed still ends succeeded {index, custom_id, status_code, request_id, body \| error, input_tokens}

Other kinds can be registered by feature modules (evaluate is one); POST with an unknown kind answers 400 and lists the available ones. A saved classifier is copied into the job at submit: the stored payload carries its labels / levels, instructions, multi_label and threshold (and snapshot_of with the name). Editing or deleting the classifier afterwards does not affect the job, queued, running or resumed, so one result set never mixes two definitions.

A row the engine rejects (for example one record over CLEF_MAX_TOKENS) does not fail the job: its row is {"index": 17, "error": "input is too long ..."}, progress.failed counts it, and the rest of the chunk is processed normally. Those failures are never silent: the job view carries a warnings entry ("3 of 100 item(s) failed; ...") and clients expose has_errors / hasErrors. Two guards stop a job whose failures are systemic (for example a model that rejects every record) instead of grinding through it: the job is failed with the item error as its message when the first 16 items of a run all failed, or when at least 90% of 50 or more items failed with one and the same message; and a job in which every item failed ends failed ("all 2 item(s) failed (...)"), never succeeded. Rows produced before the abort stay readable. A job also fails on engine crashes, or when the engine stayed unavailable for CLEF_JOB_ENGINE_WAIT_S. While the model is still loading a job waits and retries; it does not fail. Every failure is logged (job <id> (<kind>) failed: ...); the client sees only a generic message for unexpected errors.

docs.title: Job object
docs.text:
{
  "id": "job_3f9c1e7a5b2d4c60e8a1",
  "kind": "classify",
  "status": "running",
  "progress": {"done": 12000, "total": 50000, "failed": 3, "percent": 24.0},
  "eta_s": 4560.2, "items_per_s": 8.33,
  "created_at": "2026-10-03T09:00:00Z", "started_at": "2026-10-03T09:00:01Z", "finished_at": null,
  "queued_s": 1.1, "duration_s": 1440.0,
  "cancel_requested": false, "resumes": 0, "error": null,
  "result": null,
  "warnings": ["3 of 12000 item(s) failed; their result rows carry an 'error' field"],
  "metadata": {"batch": "2026-10-03"},
  "priority": "normal", "urgent": false, "schedule": null, "waiting_reason": "turn", "waiting_behind": null, "next_window_at": null,
  "expired": false, "model": "clef-flash@abc1234", "tokens": 381204,
  "webhook": {"url": "https://hooks.example.com/clef", "events": ["job.succeeded"], "has_secret": true,
              "failed_deliveries": 0,
              "deliveries": {"job.succeeded": {"id": "...", "status": "pending", "attempts": 0}}}
}

result is set when the job succeeds (classify: {items, ok, errors, by_label}, with by_labels for multi-label; score: by_level). status: "succeeded" means the job ran to the end, not that every item worked: look at progress.failed and warnings (a non-empty list also reports failed webhook deliveries). eta_s and items_per_s are measured on the current run. The webhook secret is never returned; deliveries.<event>.status is pending, delivered or failed (with attempts, last_status and last_error).

docs.title: curl
docs.text:
# submit (50k rows would go in "inputs"; raise CLEF_MAX_BODY_MB if the JSON is larger than 64 MB)
curl -sS -i http://127.0.0.1:8910/v1/jobs -H 'X-API-Key: ...' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "kind": "classify",
  "payload": {"inputs": ["Checkout is down", "Charged twice"], "labels": ["billing", "technical"]}
}'
# poll
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8910/v1/jobs/job_3f9c1e7a5b2d4c60e8a1 -H 'X-API-Key: ...'
# results: first page as JSON, or the whole thing as a CSV file
curl -sS 'http://127.0.0.1:8910/v1/jobs/job_3f9c1e7a5b2d4c60e8a1/results?limit=100' -H 'X-API-Key: ...'
curl -sS -o results.csv 'http://127.0.0.1:8910/v1/jobs/job_3f9c1e7a5b2d4c60e8a1/results?format=csv' -H 'X-API-Key: ...'

CSV columns are the flattened row (index, label, confidence, scores.billing, ...) and error last; labels lists are joined with |. Cells that start with =, +, - or @ get a leading quote so a spreadsheet does not run them as formulas. Row index is the position of the input, so you can join back to your data.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
from clef_client import ClefClient

with ClefClient() as clef:
    job = clef.classify_job(texts, ["billing", "technical", "account"])  # returns at once
    job = clef.wait_job(job.id, poll=2, on_progress=lambda j: print(j.status, j.done, j.total))
    if not job.ok:  # failed / cancelled
        raise SystemExit(job.error)
    if job.has_errors:  # succeeded, but some items failed: their rows carry .error
        print("warning:", *job.warnings, sep="\n  ")
    for item in clef.job_results(job.id):  # pages of 500, in input order
        print(item.index, item.error or item.result.label)
    clef.save_job_results(job.id, "results.csv", format="csv")  # or stream straight to disk

job.ok means the job ran to its end (succeeded); job.has_errors / job.failed / job.warnings tell you that items failed. Results are partial while the job runs: job_results() ends at the rows stored right now unless you call wait_job first or pass wait=True (it then polls until the job is finished), and save_job_results() raises JobNotFinished for an unfinished job unless require_finished=False. The file is written to <path>.part and renamed, so a failed download never leaves a truncated file. jobs() returns a list[Job] that also has .total, .limit, .offset and .has_more. redeliver_webhook(id) retries a failed webhook delivery. Pass idempotency_key= to submit_job / classify_job so a retried submit cannot duplicate the job.

AsyncClefClient has the same methods (await, and async for over job_results). Other methods: submit_job(kind, payload, webhook=..., metadata=...), job(id), jobs(status=...), cancel_job(id), delete_job(id). wait_job raises TimeoutError when timeout= passes; the job keeps running. See examples/jobs.py for a CSV in, CSV out script.

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text:
import { ClefClient } from './clients/js/src/index.js';

const clef = new ClefClient();
let job = await clef.classifyJob(texts, ['billing', 'technical', 'account']);
job = await clef.waitJob(job.id, { pollMs: 2000, onProgress: (j) => console.log(j.status, j.done, j.total) });
if (!job.ok) throw new Error(job.error);
if (job.hasErrors) console.warn(job.warnings);
for await (const item of clef.jobResults(job.id)) console.log(item.index, item.error ?? item.result.label);

Same semantics as Python: ok is "ran to its end", hasErrors / failed / warnings report failed items, jobResults is partial while the job runs ({ wait: true } polls until it is finished), and jobs() returns an array with total, limit, offset, hasMore. The client does not retry a network error after POST /v1/jobs was sent (the job might exist already); only connect errors, 429 and 503 are retried. With { idempotencyKey } the server de-duplicates, so those retries are enabled too. redeliverWebhook(id) retries a failed delivery.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
Instead of polling, pass webhook: {url, secret?, events?} when submitting. clef POSTs a JSON event when the job reaches a final state:

Event When job.succeeded, job.failed, job.cancelled the job ended (these three are the default) job.progress opt-in; at most one every 10 s, one attempt, never retried 
{"event": "job.succeeded", "delivery_id": "9b1f...", "created_at": "2026-10-03T10:00:00Z", "job": { ...the job object... }}

The body carries the job object (status, progress, result summary), not the result rows; fetch those with the API. Headers: X-Clef-Event, X-Clef-Delivery (stable across retries, use it to de-duplicate), and, when the webhook has a secret, X-Clef-Timestamp (unix seconds) and X-Clef-Signature: sha256=<hex> where the hex value is the HMAC-SHA256 of "<timestamp>.<raw body>" keyed with the secret. The signature is recomputed per attempt, so the timestamp is fresh each time.

Delivery. Any 2xx is success. 408, 425, 429, 5xx and network errors are retried with exponential backoff: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, then 120 s between attempts (CLEF_WEBHOOK_BACKOFF_S and CLEF_WEBHOOK_BACKOFF_CAP_S, +-25% jitter), up to CLEF_WEBHOOK_ATTEMPTS attempts in total (default 10, about 8 minutes, so a receiver that restarts or deploys is covered); other 4xx and every 3xx are final (redirects are never followed). Each attempt has a CLEF_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT_S (default 10) total timeout. The delivery id (X-Clef-Delivery) is minted when the final event is recorded, together with the job's state change, so it stays the same across retries and server restarts. A pending delivery survives a restart and is retried on the next start. Known behaviour: its attempt count and backoff start over then (a fresh CLEF_WEBHOOK_ATTEMPTS budget, first retry after CLEF_WEBHOOK_BACKOFF_S), so a server restarting in a loop can attempt one delivery more often than the budget. Status is in GET /v1/jobs/{id} under webhook.deliveries; webhook.failed_deliveries counts the ones that gave up, and each shows up in warnings. A finished job with a pending final event is never purged, and a failed delivery is not retried automatically: after fixing the receiver, POST /v1/jobs/{id}/webhook/redeliver (optional ?event=) sends it again with the same id and a fresh attempt budget (409 unless that delivery is failed). Webhooks are at-least-once: de-duplicate on X-Clef-Delivery.

docs.title: Verify on the receiving side
docs.text:
import hashlib, hmac, time


def verify(secret: str, headers, raw_body: bytes, tolerance_s: int = 300) -> bool:
    """headers: any case-insensitive mapping (Flask / FastAPI / requests headers). raw_body: bytes as received."""
    ts = headers["X-Clef-Timestamp"]
    if abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > tolerance_s:  # replay protection
        return False
    expected = (
        "sha256=" + hmac.new(secret.encode(), ts.encode() + b"." + raw_body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    )
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, headers["X-Clef-Signature"])

Always compute over the raw bytes (not a re-serialised JSON object), reject a missing signature when you configured a secret, and answer 2xx quickly (do the work asynchronously).

docs.title: Webhooks are off by default (SSRF)
docs.text:
A webhook makes the server send a request to an address chosen by the API caller. So the feature is disabled until the operator sets CLEF_WEBHOOK_ALLOW to a comma-separated list of what may be called:

CLEF_WEBHOOK_ALLOW='hooks.example.com,*.corp.example.net,192.168.1.0/24'
  • A hostname must be listed exactly (hooks.example.com) or by suffix (*.corp.example.net). A URL whose host is an IP literal must fall inside a listed IP or CIDR.
  • Checked at submit (400 with webhook.url: ...) and again on every delivery attempt: the hostname is resolved right then, every returned address must be public or inside a listed IP / CIDR, and the request is sent to that checked address (Host header and TLS server name keep the hostname). A DNS answer that changes between attempts (DNS rebinding) is therefore refused.
  • A private or loopback receiver (for example 192.168.1.20, or 127.0.0.1 for a local script) must be listed by IP or CIDR; listing only its hostname is not enough. Link-local (169.254.0.0/16, which includes cloud metadata endpoints), multicast, unspecified and reserved addresses are refused even if a CIDR would cover them.
  • IPv6 addresses that embed an IPv4 address (IPv4-mapped, NAT64 64:ff9b::/96 and 64:ff9b:1::/48, 6to4, Teredo) are judged by the IPv4 inside, so 64:ff9b::a00:5 is refused as the private 10.0.0.5 it translates to (listing 10.0.0.0/8 is what allows it). Site-local and reserved IPv6 ranges are refused; ::1 still works when listed.
  • Only http / https, no credentials in the URL, no redirects, no proxy settings from the environment, and an API key is never sent. Use https for anything that leaves your machine.
  • Secrets are stored in the database (clef.db in the state directory, or your CLEF_DATABASE_URL) in clear text, because HMAC needs them; protect it like the API keys file. The secret is write-only through the API.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Several jobs can be running at once (up to CLEF_JOB_ACTIVE, default 4); they take turns at the engine, one chunk at a time, so a long job from one key no longer blocks everyone else's. Every job in turns shows running in GET /v1/jobs; waiting_reason says why one is not advancing right now: turn (waiting for its chunk), behind (an older job of the same key goes first; waiting_behind is its id), active_limit (no free slot, or it gave its slot to another key's job: see Fair slots), off_hours (outside its window; next_window_at says when it opens).

Priority. "priority": "low" | "normal" (default) | "high". Classes are strict: while a high job has work, normal and low wait. A job that has not had a turn for CLEF_JOB_AGING_S (default 3600 s) moves up one class (never to urgent), so nothing starves. GET /v1/jobs?priority=high filters.

Fair share. Inside a class, turns are shared per key name (the job owner), weighted by records: two keys with one huge job each advance at the same speed, and a key with ten jobs does not get ten times the turns. Inside one key the oldest job goes first and the key's newer jobs wait (waiting_reason: "behind") until it finishes: the first results arrive sooner than if the jobs shared the turns, and the last ones no later. Send "priority": "high" to let a newer job go first. A key that comes back after being idle, or whose jobs were paused (off-hours, or waiting for a slot), starts level with the others; it does not collect the turns it missed.

Fair slots. When every slot is taken and another key's job waits for one, a key holding more than its share (CLEF_JOB_ACTIVE divided by the keys that want a slot, rounded up) gives up its newest job after that job's current chunk. The job stays running with waiting_reason: "active_limit", keeps its progress and continues when a slot is free again. A key alone in the queue still uses every slot; a high job never yields to a normal one, and urgent jobs are not counted.

Off-hours window. "schedule": {"window": "20:00-06:00", "tz": "Europe/Madrid"} restricts a job to a window (start > end crosses midnight, start == end is 24 h; tz defaults to CLEF_JOB_TZ). Without schedule, a job uses CLEF_JOB_WINDOW when it is set. Outside the window a queued job stays queued; a job that is running when the window closes finishes its current chunk, then stays running (waiting_reason: "off_hours") without taking turns or holding a slot, and continues when the window opens again. On a daylight-saving change, an edge inside the skipped hour starts at the next valid minute and an edge in the repeated hour uses the first occurrence; a window that lies entirely inside the skipped hour (say 02:15-02:45) does not open that day. A bad window or time zone is 400.

Urgent. "urgent": true needs the urgent scope (403 otherwise). The job takes the top class, ignores its window and does not wait for a free slot.

Expiry. "expire_after_s": 7200 cancels the job (status: "cancelled", error: "expired", expired: true) that long after it first could run: from submit, or, for a windowed job submitted outside its window, from the moment the window first opens. It stops between chunks; the rows already computed are kept.

Daily quota. For a key with a daily quota, the whole job (its record count) is reserved at submit, against the UTC day of the submit, even if it runs on later days: 429 daily quota exceeded when it does not fit, nothing is queued. When a job ends cancelled or failed (expiry included), the records it did not process are handed back to that day. Records answered from the result cache are not charged. A replay of an Idempotency-Key is free.

Everything above is kept in the database, so queued jobs, priorities, windows and reservations survive a restart; the fair-share counters restart from zero. A job that was paused off-hours when the server stopped resumes as interrupted and waits for its window like a queued one.

docs.title: Limits, ownership, retention
docs.text:
Setting Default Meaning CLEF_MAX_JOB_ITEMS 100000 Items per job (classify, score inputs / systemone requests). CLEF_MAX_JOBS 100 Queued + running jobs; more is 409 with Retry-After. CLEF_JOB_TTL_HOURS 168 Finished jobs (and their rows) are purged this long after they finish; 0 keeps them forever. CLEF_JOB_ENGINE_WAIT_S 600 How long a job waits for an unavailable engine before failing. CLEF_WEBHOOK_ALLOW empty Allowed webhook hosts / IPs / CIDRs; empty disables webhooks. CLEF_WEBHOOK_TIMEOUT_S 10 Total timeout of one delivery attempt. CLEF_WEBHOOK_ATTEMPTS 10 Delivery attempts for final events. CLEF_WEBHOOK_BACKOFF_S 2 First retry delay; doubles each attempt. CLEF_WEBHOOK_BACKOFF_CAP_S 120 Longest delay between two attempts. CLEF_JOB_ACTIVE 4 Jobs that take turns at once (>= 1). 1 runs them strictly one after another. CLEF_JOB_AGING_S 3600 A waiting job rises one priority class per this many seconds without a turn; 0 = no aging. CLEF_JOB_TZ UTC Time zone of job windows that give no tz, and of CLEF_JOB_WINDOW. CLEF_JOB_WINDOW empty Default window HH:MM-HH:MM for jobs without schedule; empty = always open. CLEF_JOB_MAX_RESUMES 3 A job that crashed the server (found running at startup) more often than this fails (interrupted N times, giving up); clean restarts do not count; 0 = no limit.

The request body limit (CLEF_MAX_BODY_MB, default 64) applies to POST /v1/jobs: roughly 100 000 short texts fit, 50 000 long ones may not. Media in systemone jobs counts too. Per-record limits (labels, images, tokens) are the same as for the synchronous endpoints.

Ownership. With auth off, every caller sees every job. With CLEF_API_KEY / CLEF_API_KEYS on, a job is owned by the key name that submitted it (default for CLEF_API_KEY); another key without the admin scope gets 404 for it (not 403) and does not see it in GET /v1/jobs, while a key without the jobs scope gets 403 on every /v1/jobs route. Keys with the admin scope (and the env keys, which have every scope) see all jobs, including those submitted while auth was off (no owner), which nobody else sees once auth is on. Webhook URLs and metadata are visible to the owner and to admins.

Persistence and restart. Jobs, their submitted payloads (your inputs) and result rows live in the database (SQLite <state dir>/clef.db by default, or Postgres; in clear text, see Storage) and survive restarts. Rows are written after every chunk, in one transaction that appends after the last stored row, so a chunk that was in flight when the server stopped is either stored whole or computed again: never a gap, never a duplicate. If the server stops while a job runs it is marked interrupted and, on the next start, resumed from the last stored row, ahead of queued jobs. resumes counts crashes only: a clean stop (clef stop, Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, anything that runs the shutdown) parks the job without counting it, while a job found still running at startup (the process died) counts one. A job that keeps killing the process would otherwise be resumed forever, so after CLEF_JOB_MAX_RESUMES crashes (default 3) it is failed with interrupted N times, giving up and a WARNING is logged. A job whose cancel was requested (cancel_requested: true) before a stop or crash is not resumed: it ends cancelled (with its job.cancelled webhook), at shutdown or at the next start. The final status and the pending webhook record are written in one transaction, so a crash cannot leave a finished job without its event. The built-in kinds (including evaluate) resume exactly; a custom kind that does not declare itself resumable restarts from item 0. Resuming re-reads the stored payload, which already holds the saved classifier as it was at submit. Finished jobs are purged on their own timer (every ten minutes), also while a job is running.

A job remembers the model it was submitted for ("id@revision", from the server that took it). If the server now serves another model or revision, the job fails with job was submitted for <model>, this server serves <ref> instead of mixing two models in one result set; jobs from before v3.2 have no recorded model and run as before. A model in the payload that this server does not serve is 404 at submit. With a saved classifier, the payload may also give "version": N (default: the latest); the stored snapshot records the version it copied as classifier_version.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
One database holds jobs, result rows, saved classifiers (with their versions) and the audit log; the v3.2 key, review, router and batch tables live there too. One clef server per database: Postgres is for operations (backups, one place for everything), not for several servers sharing a queue.

Setting Default Meaning CLEF_DATABASE_URL unset Unset: SQLite <state dir>/clef.db. postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/clef (or postgres://) uses Postgres and needs pip install 'clef-local[postgres]' (psycopg 3). CLEF_DATABASE_POOL_SIZE 5 Postgres connections (plus as many again under load); ignored on SQLite.
  • Upgrades are automatic. Every start runs the schema migrations (Alembic, upgrade heads) before serving. clef db current shows the schema version, clef db upgrade runs the migrations with the server stopped, and clef doctor and GET /health ("db": {"dialect", "schema_version", "url"}) report it. The password in the URL is always shown as ***.
  • From v3.1. On the first start with the default URL, <state dir>/jobs.db is copied to clef.db (once; logged) with SQLite's online backup API, and the original is renamed jobs.db.migrated (delete it once you are happy). The copy needs the file to itself: if a v3.1 server still has it open, startup (and clef db upgrade) stops with jobs.db is in use by another process; stop the old server first and changes nothing. If both clef.db and jobs.db exist, clef.db is used and a WARNING is logged. The saved classifiers in <state dir>/classifiers/*.json are imported once as version 1 of each (no owner); the folder is then renamed classifiers.imported/ (unreadable files are logged and skipped, and move there with the rest: fix one and PUT it to import it). clef classifiers export [--out DIR] [--name N] writes the latest version of each back to <DIR>/<name>.json (the v3.1 file format plus version).
  • SQLite to Postgres. Stop the server, then clef db copy --from sqlite:///<state dir>/clef.db --to postgresql://user:pass@host/clef [--yes]: every table, 1000 rows at a time, in one transaction on the target, which is migrated first and must be empty. Then start the server with CLEF_DATABASE_URL set to the target. The source is not changed; it must be at the current schema (start the server on it once, or clef db upgrade).
  • Backups. clef backup [--out PATH] copies the SQLite database with SQLite's online backup API, safe while the server runs, to <state dir>/backups/clef-<UTC time>.db (readable by you only). For Postgres it prints a pg_dump command instead (exit 2).
  • One server per database. On Postgres a server holds an advisory lock for its lifetime; a second server on the same database stops at startup with another clef server holds this database (one server per database). The server checks every 10 s that it still holds the lock; if it lost it (its database connection was cut or killed), it logs a CRITICAL line and exits with status 3 at once, so run it under a supervisor that restarts it (systemd Restart=on-failure, Docker restart: unless-stopped). The CLI commands do not take the lock. On SQLite nothing enforces it: do not point two servers at one state dir (each would recover the other's running job at startup).
  • Errors. A database that cannot be reached answers 503 database unavailable. Drop everything by deleting clef.db (SQLite) or the database (Postgres) with the server stopped.

Throughput. Up to CLEF_JOB_ACTIVE jobs take turns, one chunk at a time, at the engine's batch speed, shared with interactive traffic; priority, fair share and windows between jobs are in Scheduling. Inside the engine, job work (ctx.decide, including the evaluate kind) is in the background lane and requests (ctx.infer) in the interactive lane:

  • A micro-batch holds one class. Interactive goes first whenever any is queued, even if it arrived during a batch window opened by job work.
  • Classes are not mixed to fill a micro-batch. The model is compute-bound, so a request riding in a batch of 8 job records would wait for all 8; running it alone costs the job one extra host overhead instead.
  • Jobs are not starved by steady traffic: after CLEF_INTERACTIVE_BURST (default 8) interactive micro-batches in a row while job work waited, one job micro-batch runs. Lower it to favour jobs, raise it to favour requests.
  • Two opt-in flags raise a job's own throughput without changing any of this (one GPU worker, one job chunk in flight, interactive first): CLEF_JOB_SORT_WINDOW=N takes N items at a time and sends them to the engine sorted by token length (less padding), and CLEF_TOKENIZE_AHEAD=1 encodes the next window on CPU threads while the current one is on the GPU. Results stay in input order, rows are persisted a whole window at a time and a resume recomputes at most one window. They apply to the classify, score, systemone, evaluate and batch kinds, are off by default, and wait for a GPU measurement (Performance).
  • GET /v1/stats reports queue_depth_by_class (interactive, background) next to the total queue_depth.

Measured on the RX 7900 XTX (bf16, short tickets) before the lane existed: a 500-item classify job ran at ~15 items/s (32 s); meanwhile interactive /v1/classify calls took p50 422 / p95 458 ms instead of 109 / 118 ms idle. With the lane the wait is bounded by the job micro-batch already being computed; the new numbers are pending a GPU run.

docs.title: Writing a job kind
docs.text:
A feature module registers {"validate": fn, "run": async_fn} in ctx.extra["job_kinds"] (use setdefault). An optional "snapshot": fn(payload, parsed) -> payload rewrites what is stored at submit (the built-in kinds use it to copy a saved classifier into the payload):

def validate(payload: dict) -> Parsed: ...      # raise ValueError -> 400 at submit; return the parsed object

async def run(ctx, parsed, job) -> dict | None:
    job.set_total(len(parsed.items))
    for chunk in chunks(parsed.items, 8):
        if job.cancelled:
            return None
        await job.add_items([{"index": ..., ...}, ...])   # persist rows in order; progress += len(rows)
    return {"summary": "stored as job.result"}

Rows containing an "error" key count as failed, and the circuit breaker above applies to every kind (it raises JobAborted from add_items). Call the model with job.decide(requests) (it waits for the job's turn in the scheduler; ctx.decide directly bypasses the turns), keep one call in flight, and check job.cancelled between calls (it also turns true when the job expires). Other optional kind keys: "records": fn(parsed) -> int (records reserved from the daily quota at submit; default the length of inputs / requests) and "completed_if_all_failed": True (a run where every item failed still ends succeeded; otherwise it ends failed). job.add_items(rows, tokens=N) adds N to the job's tokens; without tokens it sums the rows' input_tokens. Add "resumable": True only if run honours job.resume_from (the number of rows already stored) and does not re-emit them.

docs.title: Running clef-flash in less memory
docs.text:
The release is ~19 GB in bf16 and a default clef serve peaks at ~19.5 GB of device memory, so out of the box the floor is a 24 GB GPU or a 32 GB Mac. Three settings lower that floor. Everything below was measured on one machine (RX 7900 XTX, ROCm 7.2, Windows 11 + WSL2, 2026-10-03); see Measured results for the numbers and Caveats for what was not tested.

You have Use Cost (measured, 7900 XTX) 24 GB GPU, 32 GB Mac nothing none 16 GB GPU CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB=15 lossless (identical probabilities); p50 +15%, throughput -12%; ~6 GB host RAM 12 GB GPU CLEF_QUANT=int8 CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu mean prob error 0.006, 2 of 399 top choices flipped; p50 +36%, throughput -13%; ~2.5 GB host RAM 12 GB GPU, lossless CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB=11 identical probabilities; p50 2.3x, throughput -29%; ~11 GB host RAM 8 GB GPU CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB=7 identical probabilities; p50 3.6x, throughput -45%; ~15 GB host RAM (a cap of 6 crashed) 24 GB Mac CLEF_QUANT=int8 ~12 GB; not validated on Apple Silicon

clef doctor reads the detected memory and prints the matching line ("memory setting").

docs.title: CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu and CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB (lossless, CUDA and ROCm)
docs.text:
Keeps part of the model in host RAM and streams it to the GPU per forward. Nothing is approximated: the weights are the same bf16 tensors, so the probabilities are bit-identical to a normal run (measured: max |dp| 0.0 on 200 records).

  1. The token embedding and the output embedding (~4 GB) never leave the host. The model only gathers rows from them (a few thousand tokens per forward), so the lookup runs on the CPU and the result is copied over. This alone frees 4 GB at a cost of microseconds.
  2. Decoder layers that do not fit under the budget stay in pinned host memory and are copied to the GPU just before they run, on a side stream, up to two layers ahead of the compute, then dropped. Streamed layers are spread evenly through the stack so resident layers hide the transfer (measured copy bandwidth ~26 GB/s on the 7900 XTX, and copies overlap compute).
  3. The vision tower, the joint head, the final norm and rotary tables always stay on the GPU.

CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB is the memory the process may allocate on the device (weights + activations). The server plans the split from it (2.5 GB is kept for activations), applies it as a hard allocator limit, and fails the load with a one-line error if even streaming every layer does not fit. 0 (default) means "whatever is free". The driver context and the desktop take about 1 GB on top, so on an N GB card use N - 1.

Only the layers you cannot fit are streamed, so the cost grows smoothly with how much you cut. Host RAM needed is the size of what was moved off the GPU (listed in the table) plus a couple of GB. CLEF_PREFLIGHT=1 checks this.

macOS and CPU: device and host share one memory pool, so offload does nothing there (a warning is logged).

docs.title: Warnings you may see
docs.text:
Settings that cannot take full effect no longer fail silently. They are logged at WARNING and listed in /health warnings (and by clef doctor):

  • CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB is not enforced (macOS / CPU share one pool, or the allocator refused the limit), or is above the free memory (the layer plan then uses the free memory), or does not shape the plan because CLEF_QUANT keeps the quantized layers on the device.
  • Pinned host memory is unavailable: streamed layers fall back to pageable copies, which is much slower.
  • CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu with CLEF_QUANT: the direct host placement was refused by transformers and the embeddings were moved after the load. Only that specific refusal falls back; a corrupt checkpoint, host out-of-memory or any other error fails the load with its own message.
  • CLEF_QUANT=nf4 on ROCm (lossy) and CLEF_QUANT=int8 on MPS (not validated): doctor shows WARN, not OK.
  • CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu with a cap below 7 GB: a 6 GB cap segfaulted at load on WSL2, so the preflight (and doctor) refuses it there and warns elsewhere. CLEF_PREFLIGHT=0 skips the check.

docs.title: CLEF_QUANT=int8 (weight-only, all backends)
docs.text:
Backend Library Notes CUDA bitsandbytes (unchanged) CLEF_QUANT_BACKEND=torchao selects torchao instead (pip install torchao). Measured on an RTX 4070 Ti: torchao is the better choice, see below ROCm torchao measured: 2x faster and 3x closer to bf16 than bitsandbytes int8 on the same GPU MPS, CPU torchao loads through the same code; not validated on hardware

Linear layers of the language model (~13 GB -> ~6.5 GB) become int8 with per-channel scales (weight-only: activations stay bf16). The embeddings, the output embedding and the vision tower stay bf16. Needs pip install torchao (it is part of the rocm, mps and cpu extras; pip install "clef-local[quant]" adds it elsewhere). Combine with CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu to also move the 4 GB of embeddings to the host: that is the 12 GB setting.

CLEF_QUANT=nf4 (bitsandbytes 4-bit) loads on ROCm too, but is not recommended: it flipped the top choice on 35 of 399 questions (~9%) in our set. Use it only if nothing else fits.

docs.title: Why not 4-bit, GGUF, AWQ, GPTQ
docs.text:
• torchao int4: needs the mslk kernel package (CUDA); it failed to load on ROCm. Not offered. The unpacked int4 variants store int8 and save nothing.
  • bitsandbytes nf4: works on ROCm, but the accuracy cost is large (table). Offered only as nf4.
  • GGUF / llama.cpp: the quantized backbone would have to be driven as an encoder whose hidden states feed the joint schema head (cross-attention over every token, per-span means, option-embedding lookups), which GGUF has no notion of. The head would have to be a separate PyTorch module fed with llama.cpp embeddings, the vision tower needs the separate mmproj path, and batching / padding semantics change. Also depends on llama.cpp's support for this Qwen3.5 Gated DeltaNet hybrid, which we did not verify. Not feasible cheaply; no parity could be measured.
  • AWQ / GPTQ: need a calibration run with a task-appropriate objective (the logits come from the joint head, not from next-token prediction, so stock calibration optimises the wrong thing), kernels that are mostly CUDA-only (Marlin/ExLlama; weak ROCm and none for MPS), and support for the hybrid linear-attention layers. Weight-only int8 already gets 12 GB with one-digit-percent probability error; the 4-bit tools would trade much more accuracy for a smaller gain. Not attempted.

docs.title: Measured results
docs.text:
RX 7900 XTX 24 GB, ROCm 7.2, torch 2.11.0+rocm7.2, WSL2 (25 GB RAM), 2026-10-03, one configuration per process, bf16 measured first and last in the same session (152 / 154 ms p50, 4.72 / 4.67 req/s: 1% drift). Workload: 200 records (choice 2-6 options, score 3-5 levels, noul; 1-3 questions each; states of ~15-1500 tokens; 10 with an image). "single" = 100 text records one at a time through Engine.decide; "c=8" = 160 requests, 8 in flight, through the engine's micro-batching. Parity = every answer option's probability against the bf16 run of the same session, one record per forward (399 questions).

Setting Device GB, peak allocated / reserved Host RAM after load single p50 / p95 req/s c=8 Max / mean abs prob diff Top-1 flips bf16 (default) 18.4 / 19.4 1.5 GB 152 / 560 ms 4.72 reference - OFFLOAD=cpu cap 16 13.8 / 15.6 5.1 GB 169 / 600 ms 4.36 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 15 13.1 / 15.0 6.2 GB 175 / 597 ms 4.15 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 12 9.8 / 12.0 9.9 GB 327 / 648 ms 3.47 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 11 9.0 / 11.0 11.1 GB 343 / 634 ms 3.37 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 8 5.8 / 8.0 14.3 GB 498 / 667 ms 2.80 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 7 5.1 / 7.0 15.0 GB 540 / 671 ms 2.59 0 / 0 0 / 399 OFFLOAD=cpu cap 6 crashed (segfault while loading; 28 layers pinned on WSL2) QUANT=int8 (torchao) 12.0 / 12.9 1.5 GB 198 / 595 ms 4.23 0.062 / 0.0058 2 / 399 QUANT=int8 OFFLOAD=cpu (embeddings on host) 8.3 / 9.2 2.5 GB 206 / 611 ms 4.10 0.062 / 0.0058 2 / 399 QUANT=int8 QUANT_BACKEND=bnb (bitsandbytes) 11.6 / 12.7 2.5 GB 420 / 680 ms 3.01 0.262 / 0.0175 22 / 399 QUANT=nf4 (bitsandbytes) 8.5 / 9.2 1.5 GB 249 / 637 ms 3.66 0.449 / 0.0329 35 / 399 fp16 (noise floor, separate run, 200 text records) 18.2 / 18.4 159 ms (bf16 that run: 176) 0.021 / 0.0019 0 / 399
  • The cap is enforced on the PyTorch allocator. The whole process (reserved memory + driver context) measured about 0.65 GB above the cap, so use N - 1 GB for an N GB card: 15 for 16 GB, 11 for 12 GB, 7 for 8 GB.
  • Host RAM after load is the process RSS once the model is in place: the pinned copies of everything that was moved off the GPU. During loading RSS peaks higher (up to ~19 GB) because the safetensors files are memory-mapped; those pages are reclaimable page cache.
  • p95 is dominated by the longest records of the eval set (~1500 tokens), which are compute-bound and unaffected by the settings; p50 is the number that moves.
  • Offload latency is the PCIe copy of the streamed layers (about 0.43 GB per layer at ~26 GB/s) partly hidden behind compute; batching amortises it (req/s at c=8 falls less than single latency rises).
  • int8 flips: 2 of 399 questions changed their top option, against 0 for fp16 vs bf16. The mean probability error 0.006 is ~3x the fp16/bf16 noise floor.

docs.title: int8 on CUDA: torchao measured better than the default
docs.text: On an RTX 4070 Ti (12 GB, WSL2, QUANT=int8 OFFLOAD=cpu, 200 records, against the lossless offload run) torchao gave a mean probability error of 0.0057 and 3 of 399 flipped answers at p50 170 ms. The auto choice, bitsandbytes, gave 0.0172 and 22 of 399 at p50 232 ms, and failed the batch-versus-single integration test. These match the ROCm numbers for the same backends. If you run int8 on an NVIDIA card, set CLEF_QUANT_BACKEND=torchao (results).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• One machine, one day, one model. Same-day drift is ~5%; every row was measured back to back in one session against the bf16 reference of that session.
  • CUDA was run on one card, an RTX 4070 Ti (12 GB, WSL2), in the int8 and offload modes: see hardware-results.md. nf4 matched the ROCm numbers (36 of 399 flips on CUDA). Plain bf16 and other CUDA cards are untested, and so are Apple Silicon, MPS and CPU torchao. Please run bench/memory_bench.py there and add the rows to docs/hardware-results.md.
  • A 12 GB card is shared with the desktop (about 1.2 GB on Windows), so the usable cap there is lower than N - 1.
  • bench/memory_bench.py needs a reference run for parity. Without a card big enough for bf16, use the lossless offload run (--offload cpu --max-device-gb <N-2>) as --save-reference.
  • OFFLOAD=cpu refuses to start unless the free host RAM exceeds the weights kept on the host by about 2 GB. On WSL2 with 32 GB, raise memory= in .wslconfig (21 GB worked for the lossless modes on a 12 GB card).
  • The cap limits what PyTorch allocates, not the driver context (~0.5-1 GB) or other processes.
  • Offload needs host RAM (table). On WSL2, size the VM (.wslconfig memory=) accordingly.
  • Offload and long inputs: activations for a very long record (thousands of tokens, batch 8) can exceed the 2.5 GB reserve; the request then fails with a 503 GpuOutOfMemory and the server stays up. Lower CLEF_MAX_MICROBATCH or raise the cap.
  • Media requests are served the same way. The vision tower stays on the GPU (0.9 GB).
  • The server's text/media parity above comes from bench/memory_bench.py (200 records: choice 2-6 options, score 3-5 levels, noul; 1-3 questions each; states of ~15-1500 tokens; 10 image records), one record per forward.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
python bench/memory_bench.py --label bf16 --dtype bfloat16 --save-reference bench/out/ref_bf16.json
python bench/memory_bench.py --label off15 --offload cpu --max-device-gb 15 --reference bench/out/ref_bf16.json
python bench/memory_bench.py --label int8off --quant int8 --offload cpu --reference bench/out/ref_bf16.json
python bench/parity.py --quant int8 --dtype bfloat16     # same eval set, loads bf16 itself as the reference

One configuration per process (device memory is only meaningful that way). Stop any running clef server first.

docs.title: OpenAI and Hugging Face compatibility
docs.text:
clef speaks two familiar dialects so existing tools can use it without code changes:

  • OpenAI: GET /v1/models, POST /v1/chat/completions (structured outputs and forced function calls), and /v1/files + /v1/batches (the Batch API).
  • Hugging Face Inference API: zero-shot classification at POST /hf/models/{model_id}.

Both sit on the same engine and the same infer path as /v1/systemone: same API keys, same rate limit, same request log and stats, same limits (CLEF_MAX_QUESTIONS, CLEF_MAX_LABELS, ...). Each request is one SystemOne record, so the probabilities are identical to the equivalent /v1/systemone call.

What clef is, and is not

clef-flash is a decision model. Given an input and a set of options it returns a calibrated probability for every option in one forward pass; it does not generate text. That is a great fit for routing, triage, moderation, tagging, ratings and gating, and the wrong tool for chat, summaries or code.

So a chat completion here is a structured output: you describe the decisions you want as a JSON schema (enums, booleans, integer scales) and clef answers each one. A request with no usable schema gets a clear 400 explaining this instead of a made-up reply.

docs.title: OpenAI SDK
docs.text:
Point the SDK at /v1 and use any API key (or your CLEF_API_KEY, sent as Authorization: Bearer).

from typing import Literal
from openai import OpenAI
from pydantic import BaseModel

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8910/v1", api_key="not-needed")


class Triage(BaseModel):
    team: Literal["billing", "technical", "account"]
    outage: bool


r = client.beta.chat.completions.parse(
    model="clef-flash",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You triage support tickets."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Checkout is down, orders blocked"},
    ],
    response_format=Triage,
)
print(r.choices[0].message.parsed)  # Triage(team='technical', outage=True)

Plain JSON schema works the same way, and curl needs nothing but JSON:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8910/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "clef-flash",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Checkout is down"}],
  "response_format": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": "triage", "schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "team": {"type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "technical"], "description": "Who handles it?"},
      "outage": {"type": "boolean", "description": "Is a service down?"}
    }}}}
}'

{"id": "chatcmpl-...", "object": "chat.completion", "model": "clef-flash",
 "choices": [{"index": 0, "finish_reason": "stop", "logprobs": null,
              "message": {"role": "assistant", "content": "{\"team\": \"technical\", \"outage\": true}"}}],
 "usage": {"prompt_tokens": 120, "completion_tokens": 0, "total_tokens": 120},
 "clef": {"questions": {"team": {"type": "choice", "value": "technical", "confidence": 0.96,
                                 "probabilities": {"billing": 0.04, "technical": 0.96}},
                        "outage": {"type": "bool", "value": true, "confidence": 0.97,
                                   "probabilities": {"true": 0.97, "false": 0.03}}},
          "timing": {"forward_ms": 141.2, "total_ms": 150.3}, "request_id": "..."}}

LangChain and similar frameworks only need the base URL and a structured-output call. Verified with langchain-openai 1.7.1 and langchain-core 1.6.10 (2026-10-12) against a live server: with_structured_output(Triage) (the default json_schema method) and method="function_calling" both return the right object. method="json_mode" and a plain invoke() carry no schema, so they get the 400 missing_schema described above:

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI

llm = ChatOpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8910/v1", api_key="not-needed", model="clef-flash")
triage = llm.with_structured_output(Triage)
print(triage.invoke("Checkout is down, orders blocked"))

Any tool with an "OpenAI-compatible endpoint" setting works the same way: base URL http://127.0.0.1:8910/v1, model clef-flash. The tool just has to ask for structured output.

docs.title: How a request maps to clef
docs.text: OpenAI clef messages the SystemOne state (see below) image_url content parts (data URLs) images video_url content parts (non-standard, as in vLLM) videos response_format.json_schema.schema one question per top-level property tools + tool_choice naming one function the function's parameters schema, same rules; answer returned as tool_calls logprobs / top_logprobs log(p) of each option (below) usage clef usage (completion_tokens is always 0)

docs.title: Messages become the state
docs.text:
A lone user message is passed through verbatim. Anything else becomes a readable transcript, in order, one blank line between turns:

system: You triage support tickets.

user: Checkout is down

assistant: Noted.

user: Still down

Assistant and tool turns are kept because they are context for the decision (developer is read as system, function as tool; an assistant tool call shows as [called name(args)]). Text parts of a content array are joined with newlines. Audio and file parts are rejected with a 400.

Images follow the same rules as everywhere else: data: URLs always, http(s) URLs only when CLEF_ALLOW_URL_FETCH=1.

docs.title: Schema properties become questions
docs.text:
Each top-level property of the schema is one decision. required, additionalProperties, strict and name are ignored (every property is always answered). $ref/$defs, allOf with one entry, Optional (anyOf with null) and unions of constants are resolved, so schemas generated by Pydantic work as they are.

Property clef question Value returned {"type": "string", "enum": [...]} (2+ options), a Literal, an Enum choice the most likely option {"type": "boolean"} noul (yes/no) true when P(yes) >= 0.5 {"type": "integer", "enum": [1, 2, 3]} score over the sorted values the most likely value (an integer) {"type": "integer", "minimum": a, "maximum": b} (2..64 values) score over a..b the most likely integer string enum with "x-clef-ordinal": true score, options in the order given the most likely option {"type": "array", "items": {"enum": [...]}} one noul per option (multi-label) the options with P >= CLEF_CLASSIFY_THRESHOLD (0.5), best first

The property description becomes the question's instructions, and a description at the top of the schema (or the function description for tools) is placed in front of every question. Option descriptions help the model when the option names are ambiguous. Two ways to give them, both plain JSON schema:

{"type": "string", "x-clef-descriptions": {"billing": "Payments, invoices, refunds", "technical": "Bugs, outages"},
 "enum": ["billing", "technical"]}

{"oneOf": [{"const": "billing", "description": "Payments, invoices, refunds"},
           {"const": "technical", "description": "Bugs, outages"}]}

For integer scales the keys of x-clef-descriptions are the numbers as text ({"1": "Can wait", "3": "Today"}). x-clef-* keywords are clef extensions and are ignored by everything else; with Pydantic, set them through Field(json_schema_extra={"x-clef-ordinal": True}).

choice vs score

Use score (integer enum, bounded integer, or x-clef-ordinal) when the options are ordered, such as low/medium/high or 1-5 stars; clef then reasons about the ordering. Use plain enums for unordered categories.

Properties clef cannot decide (free-form string, number, nested object, ...) are rejected with a 400 whose param points at the property, for example response_format.json_schema.schema.properties.summary.

docs.title: Forced function calls
docs.text: tools with one function and tool_choice set to that function (or "required", or "auto" with a single tool) returns a tool_calls message whose arguments is the JSON object, exactly like a model that obeyed the call. The finish_reason is "stop" when the function was named in tool_choice (as OpenAI does) and "tool_calls" otherwise. clef cannot decide whether or which of several tools to call: with several tools, name one in tool_choice (a 400 says so otherwise). tool_choice: "none" ignores the tools. If both a forced tool and a response_format are sent, the tool wins.

docs.title: Logprobs and probabilities
docs.text:
With "logprobs": true, choices[0].logprobs.content has one token-like entry per decision (per option for arrays): token is the chosen value as text, logprob is log(p) of it. top_logprobs: N (0..64) adds the best N options of that decision with their log(p), so exp(logprob) recovers clef's calibrated probability. Without top_logprobs the lists are empty, as in OpenAI. Probabilities that round to zero are reported as -9999.

The non-standard top-level clef field always has the full picture: per property the type, value, confidence and all probabilities ({"true": ..., "false": ...} for booleans, option -> probability otherwise), plus timing and request_id. The official SDKs expose unknown fields (response.model_extra["clef"] in Python).

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: "stream": true returns valid Server-Sent Events: a chat.completion.chunk with the role, one with the whole JSON as content (or the tool_calls entry), one with finish_reason, then data: [DONE]. A decision is a single forward pass, so there is nothing to stream token by token. stream_options: {"include_usage": true} adds the usage chunk. Validation errors still come back as a normal JSON error response, before any chunk.

docs.title: Supported and ignored parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Behaviour model accepted and ignored: always served by clef-flash (so hard-coded names like gpt-4o-mini work) messages required; see above response_format json_schema required (unless a tool is used); text and json_object give a 400 explaining why tools, tool_choice one function, forced; type: "function" only logprobs, top_logprobs supported (above); top_logprobs needs logprobs: true stream, stream_options.include_usage supported n 1 only; n > 1 is a 400 (a decision is deterministic, there is nothing to sample) temperature, top_p, max_tokens, max_completion_tokens, stop, seed, presence_penalty, frequency_penalty, logit_bias, user, metadata, store, parallel_tool_calls, reasoning_effort, service_tier, ... accepted and ignored functions, function_call (legacy) not supported; use tools

Ignored fields are not silent: a chat response (and the final stream chunk) carries the non-standard clef.ignored list naming each ignored field the request sent, e.g. ["model", "temperature", "max_tokens"] (model appears only when it is not clef-flash; the list is [] when nothing was ignored). The same list is logged at DEBUG. Clients that send a fixed model name keep working, and you can see that the name was not used.

GET /v1/models lists clef-flash; GET /v1/models/clef-flash returns it and any other id gives a 404 (model_not_found).

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors on the OpenAI routes use OpenAI's shape so SDKs raise their usual exceptions (BadRequestError, AuthenticationError, RateLimitError, ...):

{"error": {"message": "...", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": "n", "code": "unsupported_value"}}

Status codes match the rest of the API: 400 bad request or schema, 401 missing/invalid key (code: invalid_api_key), 404 unknown model, 413 too large, 429 rate limited (with Retry-After, type: rate_limit_error), 503 model loading or GPU out of memory. The request id is in the X-Request-ID header. The native /v1/* routes keep {detail, request_id}.

docs.title: Files and batches (the OpenAI Batch API)
docs.text:
/v1/files and /v1/batches follow OpenAI's Batch API, so the openai SDK's client.files and client.batches work unchanged. A batch is one async job of kind batch (it shows up in GET /v1/jobs?kind=batch), so it shares the job queue, the daily quota, resume after a restart and the retention timer. All routes need the jobs scope and are private to the key that created them (an admin sees every file and batch). Errors use the OpenAI shape, {"error": {"message", "type", "param", "code"}}.

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="...")
f = client.files.create(file=open("requests.jsonl", "rb"), purpose="batch")
batch = client.batches.create(input_file_id=f.id, endpoint="/v1/chat/completions", completion_window="24h")
# poll client.batches.retrieve(batch.id) until status is completed, then
print(client.files.content(batch.output_file_id).text)

docs.title: The input file
docs.text:
One JSON object per line (blank lines are ignored), at most min(CLEF_MAX_BATCH_LINES, CLEF_MAX_JOB_ITEMS) lines (50,000 by default), up to CLEF_MAX_FILE_MB (200):

{"custom_id": "ticket-1", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/chat/completions", "body": {"messages": [...], "response_format": {...}}}

custom_id is unique, method is POST and url equals the batch's endpoint. The supported endpoints are /v1/chat/completions, /v1/classify and /v1/score; each body is exactly what that route takes, with the same validation, the same limits and the same probabilities. (stream: true is not allowed in a batch.) The SDK does not check endpoint; clef answers 400 with param: "endpoint" for any other value.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Route POST /v1/files multipart: file (.jsonl), purpose=batch, optional expires_after[anchor]=created_at and expires_after[seconds] (3600..2592000). Streamed to disk; the body limit of this route alone is CLEF_MAX_FILE_MB GET /v1/files after, limit (default 20), order (desc), purpose; cursor list GET /v1/files/{id}, GET /v1/files/{id}/content the file object; the JSONL, streamed DELETE /v1/files/{id} uploaded files only. A batch's output / error file is deleted with its job (DELETE /v1/jobs/{job_id}); an input file an unfinished batch still reads is 409

Uploads expire after expires_after or CLEF_FILE_TTL_HOURS (30 days). The output and error files are not copies: they are streamed from the job's result rows, so they cost no disk and live as long as the job (CLEF_JOB_TTL_HOURS).

docs.title: Batches
docs.text:
Route POST /v1/batches input_file_id, endpoint, completion_window ("24h"), optional metadata (<= 16 string pairs; keys <= 64, values <= 512 characters) and extra_body={"clef": {...}} GET /v1/batches/{id}, GET /v1/batches the batch; newest first, after, limit 1..100 POST /v1/batches/{id}/cancel cancelling while a running chunk finishes, then cancelled; a queued batch is cancelled at once. 409 when it already ended

status is in_progress, cancelling, completed, failed, expired or cancelled, with OpenAI's timestamps and request_counts (completed = succeeded, failed = non-2xx lines). usage.input_tokens is the sum over the lines. expires_at is 24 hours after the batch is eligible to run: its creation time, or the next time its window opens when clef.schedule (or CLEF_JOB_WINDOW) holds it back. A batch not finished by then ends expired.

  • A file that is structurally wrong (a line that is not JSON, a duplicate or missing custom_id, a wrong url or method, too many lines, an empty file) makes POST /v1/batches return a batch with status failed and errors.data = [{code, line, message, param}] (at most 100). No job runs and nothing is charged.
  • A request that cannot run (a schema with no decisions, n > 1, an unknown model, a label set over the limit) is a line of the error file with its OpenAI error body and status code; the batch still ends completed, even when every line failed.
  • output_file_id appears once the batch ended with at least one success, error_file_id when a line failed or never ran. Output is in input order: {"id": "batch_req_...", "custom_id", "response": {"status_code", "request_id", "body"}, "error": null}. For a cancelled, expired or failed batch the error file also names, with {"response": null, "error": {"code": "batch_cancelled" | "batch_expired" | "batch_failed", "message"}}, every line that never ran; those custom ids are read back from the input file, which is why it cannot be deleted while the batch is unfinished.
  • A batch that stops for a systemic reason (the engine went away, the circuit breaker) is failed with errors.data = [{"code": "server_error", ...}]; the rows it did produce are still served.

The clef extension, extra_body={"clef": {"priority": "low", "urgent": false, "schedule": {"window": "20:00-06:00", "tz": "Europe/Madrid"}}} (priority low|normal|high), is the job scheduler's: the batch is queued, ordered and windowed like any job. urgent needs the urgent scope (403 otherwise). The daily quota of the key is reserved when the batch is created (429 insufficient_quota when it does not fit; a failed or cancelled batch gets the unprocessed part back).

Variable Default Meaning CLEF_MAX_FILE_MB 200 body limit of POST /v1/files only (every other route keeps CLEF_MAX_BODY_MB) CLEF_MAX_BATCH_LINES 50000 requests per batch (also capped by CLEF_MAX_JOB_ITEMS) CLEF_FILE_TTL_HOURS 720 how long an uploaded file is kept unless it has expires_after; 0 = forever

Not supported: other purpose values (assistants, fine-tune...), other endpoints, completion_window other than 24h, output_expires_after (ignored), /v1/batches from a file that another key uploaded (404, admins too).

docs.title: Hugging Face zero-shot classification
docs.text:
POST /hf/models/{model_id} (also POST /models/{model_id}) takes the Inference API body. model_id is ignored: any value, even an unknown one, is served by clef-flash (no error, no warning), and it may contain slashes (facebook/bart-large-mnli).

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8910/hf/models/clef-flash -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "inputs": "Checkout is down, orders blocked",
  "parameters": {"candidate_labels": ["billing", "technical", "account"], "multi_label": false}
}'

{"sequence": "Checkout is down, orders blocked",
 "labels": ["technical", "billing", "account"], "scores": [0.94, 0.04, 0.02]}
Field Behaviour inputs a string, or a list of strings (answered in one micro-batched pass, a list of results back; max CLEF_MAX_BATCH) parameters.candidate_labels list of strings, or a comma-separated string; de-duplicated; 2+ labels (1+ with multi_label) parameters.multi_label false (default): one label, scores sum to 1. true: independent yes/no per label, scores do not sum to 1 parameters.hypothesis_template must contain {}. clef has no NLI hypothesis step, so the filled template ("This is about billing.") is used as that label's description instead options, other fields ignored

Labels and scores are sorted by score, best first. Errors are {"error": "message"} with the usual status codes.

docs.title: Using huggingface_hub
docs.text:
InferenceClient posts to the model URL as given, so pass the full route as the model:

from huggingface_hub import InferenceClient

client = InferenceClient(
    model="http://127.0.0.1:8910/hf/models/clef-flash", token="your CLEF_API_KEY or None"
)
for item in client.zero_shot_classification("Checkout is down", ["billing", "technical", "account"]):
    print(item.label, item.score)

Two response shapes

The classic Inference API answers {"sequence", "labels", "scores"} (the default here). huggingface_hub 1.x expects the newer [{"label", "score"}, ...] list. clef detects hf_hub/1.x in the User-Agent and answers in that shape automatically. For any other client, force a shape with ?format=classic or ?format=list.

Verified against huggingface_hub 1.33 (single and multi-label, hypothesis_template) with the model=<full URL> form above. Pointing HF_ENDPOINT at the server is not supported: the library may try Hub lookups for the model id first, which clef does not serve.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No free text. There is no way to ask clef to write, summarize or explain. If your tool only sends plain chat messages, it will get the 400 that explains the schema requirement; configure it for structured output, or call /v1/classify directly.
  • Only top-level properties are decisions; nested objects and free-form strings are not supported.
  • One choice per property (argmax). The full distribution is in the clef field and in logprobs.
  • n, sampling parameters and token limits have no meaning for a single forward pass and are ignored or rejected as listed above.
  • Nullability is ignored: an Optional[...] property is always decided.
  • Streaming delivers the finished decision in one chunk.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
Measured on the AMD RX 7900 XTX (ROCm 7.2, WSL2, bf16), 2026-10-18: records of ~330 tokens, clef bench, 100 requests per level, one session (details: hardware results).
