flags off ROCm defaults (TunableOp + MASK_FREE + FAST_HEAD) Single record p50 / p95 137 / 145 ms 104 / 108 ms Throughput, concurrency 1 7.2 req/s 9.5 req/s Throughput, concurrency 8 8.8 req/s 10.9-11.3 req/s Throughput, concurrency 16 (micro-batching) 9.0 req/s 11.1-11.8 req/s Mixed-length traffic, concurrency 1-16 5.9-6.2 req/s 7.6-7.9 req/s Peak VRAM ~21.7 GB ~21.0 GB

Compute-bound

GEMMs are 81-84% of GPU kernel time, so batching adds only ~25% throughput, and the fastest lever on ROCm is better GEMM kernels (TunableOp below). A ~330-token single-record forward is GPU-bound too: kernel time is ~78% of wall time without the profiler (68 of 88 ms). With CLEF_MASK_FREE (the ROCm default) the backbone captures into a HIP graph, but replay only helps short records (64 tokens: 43 → 32 ms; 384 tokens: no gain). Padding text batches to a multiple of 64 beats both raw lengths and full buckets (CLEF_PAD_MULTIPLE); that was measured on ROCm only. NVIDIA, Mac and CPU numbers are pending hardware.

docs.title: Sharing the GPU with jobs
docs.text: Requests and jobs share one model and one worker thread. The engine queue has two lanes: requests are interactive, job chunks are background, and the next micro-batch is interactive whenever a request waits (one class per forward; after CLEF_INTERACTIVE_BURST interactive micro-batches in a row, one job micro-batch runs). A request during a job still waits for the job micro-batch already being computed (one forward per length bucket or media record in it). Measured on the 7900 XTX (unique requests, cache off): interactive p50 140 ms idle and ~625 ms during a 3000-item job, with one job or with 2 keys x 2 jobs: about one batch-8 forward (Jobs).

docs.title: Speedups: on by default on ROCm
docs.text:
Two flags and TunableOp. With the ROCm backend all three are on by default (measured on the RX 7900 XTX: TunableOp +27-32% req/s on mixed-length traffic, the two flags another +5-12% on top); on CUDA, MPS and CPU the two flags stay off until someone measures them there (bench/perf_check.sh), and TunableOp only exists on ROCm builds of PyTorch. 0 turns each one off, 1 forces a flag on. With both flags off the code path is the release's own ClefModel.forward (CPU results are byte-identical). The flags only apply to the clef-release adapter (clef-flash, clef).

With all three on, probabilities move by up to ~0.03 (different kernels sum in a different order); in the 399-question parity set no top answer changed, and with TunableOp alone the 3 that did were near coin flips (top-2 margin below 0.02). Accuracy on the 47 labelled tickets: 0.872 either way.

Flag What it does Exact? CLEF_MASK_FREE=1 Text-only batches call the backbone with attention_mask=None; the head gets a CPU-built mask, so it takes the lengths without a device sync. Removes the syncs in transformers' mask helpers (torch.all(mask == 1) in the linear-attention path, the SDPA causal check), the blocker for graph capture. Yes in exact arithmetic: the model is causal, position t reads only <= t, and the engine pads on the right, so real positions never see padding. The head slices [:length] and takes hidden[length-1] as the global vector, so it never reads padded positions either. Not applied (and not exact) for media batches (rope positions and the visual-token scatter read the mask), left padding or masks with holes. Real positions can still differ in the last bits (a different SDPA kernel for is_causal), hence the parity gate. CLEF_FAST_HEAD=1 A batch-vectorised, sync-free joint head (fast_joint_head in models/clef_release.py): index tables are built on the CPU from the encodings and sent in one transfer, span means are segment sums, ragged question and option sets are padded grids with key-padding masks, logits come back in one device-to-host copy. It reads the release head's weights; the model directory is untouched. The segment-mean formulation follows vLLM's Apache-2.0 ClefFlash head (vllm-project/vllm#61308); the code is an independent rewrite. Same maths as the release head, different loop structure. Tests compare it with the release head on random tensors: max difference below 1e-5 in fp32 (and about one bf16 ulp in bf16).

Measured (fixed-length records): the two flags +2-4% req/s alone, +5-12% with TunableOp, and a lower p95 under load (c=8 p95 776 vs 1186 ms with TunableOp). Full table: hardware results.

docs.title: TunableOp (ROCm)
docs.text:
TunableOp (on by default with ROCm builds; CLEF_TUNABLEOP=0 turns it off) makes PyTorch autotune each GEMM shape once and remember the winner. The tuned kernels are written to <state_dir>/tunableop/<model>@<rev8>/tunableop_0.csv and reloaded on the next start.

TunableOp picks, for every GEMM shape clef runs, the fastest kernel this GPU, driver, ROCm and PyTorch offer (on the 7900 XTX mostly rocBLAS solutions that rocBLAS's own default does not pick: ~40% faster GEMMs, +27-32% req/s on mixed-length traffic). It does not change the model. The results are tied to those versions: torch checks them and tunes again after an upgrade.

  1. clef serve. The server loads the tuned file, runs the normal short warmup and is ready in seconds, with the default kernels for anything not tuned yet. A live request never tunes.
  2. In the background it records the GEMMs it produces (it runs every text-batch shape up to 1024 tokens, each padded length at every batch size, once it has been quiet for CLEF_TUNABLEOP_IDLE_S, 2 s) and starts a separate tuner process (python -m clef_server.tuner, log in tuner.log next to the tuned file). The tuner is paused (SIGSTOP) the moment a request arrives and resumed once it is quiet again, so a request never waits for it; the server reloads the tuned file whenever it changes, so each tuned GEMM speeds up the next forward. The tuner writes <state_dir>/tunableop/<model>@<rev8>/tunableop_0.csv (it owns the file) and lists the GEMMs it cannot tune in tunableop_skip.csv. All of it takes about an hour of idle time on the 7900 XTX (the grid gave 535 GEMMs and 61 min on the first measured run: rocBLAS has many candidate kernels per GEMM, some take 30 s); progress is in /v1/stats (tunableop: phase discovering / tuning / done, tuned, pending, tuner running / paused). Later starts only read the file: keep the state dir (a Docker volume) and this happens once per GPU / driver / ROCm / PyTorch version.
  3. GEMMs that live traffic ran untuned (a long text, a record with images) are recorded in tunableop_untuned0.csv and tuned the same way; clef stop && clef tune does it offline.
  4. Delete the directory to re-tune from scratch.

clef sets a small budget per candidate kernel (PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_MAX_TUNING_DURATION_MS=5, PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_MAX_TUNING_ITERATIONS=20); the time is mostly a fixed cost per candidate, so a smaller budget barely helps and torch's own 30 ms / 100 picks the same kernels. CLEF_TUNABLEOP_ONLINE=1 keeps the old behaviour (every new shape is tuned on its first request, a latency spike of seconds).

docs.title: The GPU check
docs.text:
PY=~/venvs/clef/bin/python bash bench/perf_check.sh        # QUICK=1 for a ~15 min smoke

It runs the batch-8 profile (is batched serving GEMM-bound?), engine parity for each flag against the flags-off run (PASS = 0 top-1 flips and max |dp| <= 2e-3), clef bench at c=1/8/16 for each flag and both, and TunableOp on vs off (the baseline sets every flag to 0, so the defaults do not leak in). Output is in bench/out/perf/ (summary.md has the PASS/FAIL and speed tables). Run it on another GPU before turning the flags on there, and copy the numbers into hardware results. On the 7900 XTX every variant "fails" the strict 2e-3 gate with 0-3 coin-flip changes; the drift was accepted for the speed.

docs.title: Job throughput: length sort and tokenize ahead (measured: both stay off)
docs.text:
Batch jobs feed the engine in micro-batches of CLEF_MAX_MICROBATCH (default 8) in input order, so one forward can mix a 60-token and a 900-token record and pays the padding of the longest. Two opt-in flags change how a job is fed. Both are off by default: on the RX 7900 XTX the window gave +13-14% job throughput but a worse interactive p95 (926 vs ~750 ms), and tokenize-ahead gave nothing (+0.3%). The result rows, their order and the cache behaviour are the same either way.

Flag What it does CLEF_JOB_SORT_WINDOW=N (0 = off; 256-1024 recommended) The job takes N items at a time, encodes them all on CPU threads, sorts the ones that need a forward by token length and sends them to the engine in micro-batches of CLEF_MAX_MICROBATCH, so each forward carries similar lengths. Results go back to input order and the window is persisted in one write. CLEF_TOKENIZE_AHEAD=1 While a window is on the GPU, the next one is encoded on CPU threads (one micro-batch when the sort is off). Still ONE GPU worker and ONE job micro-batch in flight; interactive requests keep going first.

What to expect, and what changes:

  • Progress and job.progress webhooks move once per window instead of once per micro-batch, and a clean stop, crash or cancel inside a window recomputes (or drops) at most that window. Rows are never persisted out of order, so results stay gap-free and resume works as before.
  • Sorting only changes padding, so probabilities can differ in the last bits (a different batch composition); labels should not change. sort_check.sh reports label agreement with the flags-off run.
  • With CLEF_TOKENIZE_AHEAD=1 the next window's cache lookup happens before the current window's results are stored, so a record repeated in the next window is computed again (same result, different cache statistics).
  • A record the engine rejects, a GPU OOM or a failed encode falls back to the usual per-record isolation.

docs.title: The GPU run
docs.text:
PY=~/venvs/clef/bin/python bash bench/sort_check.sh    # QUICK=1 for a ~5 min smoke, SWEEP=1 adds 256/1024

It starts a fresh server per variant (base, sort with window 512, tokenize ahead, both; TunableOp and the speed flags off so only the feeding changes) with the result cache off, submits one classify job of 2000 long-tailed-length inputs three times after a warm-up job, probes interactive latency every 2 s, and prints items/s, gain over base, label agreement and a verdict (bench/out/sort/summary.md). Flip a default only if the median gain is over 10% and above the base spread, labels agree and interactive p95 did not get worse.

Variant Items/s Gain vs base Label agreement Interactive p95 Verdict base (flags off) 9.5-9.7 - - 734-805 ms - CLEF_JOB_SORT_WINDOW=512 10.7-11.0 +13-14% 100% 786-926 ms off (p95) CLEF_TOKENIZE_AHEAD=1 9.5 +0.3% 100% 789 ms off both 10.6 +12% 100% 1005 ms off (p95)

docs.title: Smaller-memory modes
docs.text:
Same GPU, same session, 200 mixed records (bench/memory_bench.py). Offload is lossless: the probabilities are bit-identical to bf16. Full table, method and caveats: Smaller GPUs.

Setting Device GB (peak allocated) single p50 req/s at concurrency 8 Max / mean abs probability difference bf16 (default) 18.4 152 ms 4.72 reference CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu, cap 15 (16 GB card) 13.1 175 ms 4.15 0 / 0 CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu, cap 11 (12 GB card) 9.0 343 ms 3.37 0 / 0 CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu, cap 7 (8 GB card) 5.1 540 ms 2.59 0 / 0 CLEF_QUANT=int8 + CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu (12 GB card) 8.3 206 ms 4.10 0.062 / 0.0058

Offload latency is the PCIe copy of the layers kept in host RAM, partly hidden behind compute, and it needs host RAM (about 6, 11 and 15 GB for the three caps). On NVIDIA and Apple Silicon these modes are untested on hardware.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: Tool Use clef bench HTTP load test against the running server (realistic) bench/bench.py in-process, needs the GPU bench/profile_forward.py torch.profiler bench/parity.py probability parity across dtypes and quantization, and engine parity (--engine-dump / --compare) bench/perf_check.sh the D2 GPU check: profile, parity per flag, clef bench A/B, TunableOp on/off; PASS/FAIL table bench/memory_bench.py one smaller-memory setting per process: device and host memory, latency, parity against a saved bf16 reference bench/vllm/vllm_check.sh vLLM vs clef (measured on the 7900 XTX, see below; re-run on other GPUs)

docs.title: vLLM benchmark
docs.text:
vLLM serves clef-flash natively through its own /v1/systemone (vllm-project/vllm#61308, merged 2026-10-13, nightly images only; not in the v0.32.0 release). bench/vllm/vllm_check.sh runs clef (flags off, the two flags, TunableOp) and a pinned vllm/vllm-openai-rocm nightly container on the same records at concurrency 1, 8, 16 and 32, checks parity against clef and prints a decision table. The proposed rule: parity, at least 1.3x req/s at concurrency 16, and p95 no worse.

On the RX 7900 XTX (2026-10-18) vLLM reached 12.2 req/s at concurrency 8-32 against 10.9-11.1 for tuned clef (+10%), but single requests were slower (p95 157 against 108 ms) and its probabilities differ more (max |dp| 0.034). Not adopted on this card. The check stays in the repo because another GPU (CUDA, MI300) may behave differently: run it there before deciding. On ROCm under WSL the container needs ROCPROFILER_REGISTER_ENABLED=0 (set by the script) and, with snap Docker, the WSL files copied under $HOME (DXCORE, ROCDXG, DIDS); TUN_STATE reuses an already tuned clef state dir for the TunableOp line. Details and sources: bench/vllm/README.md; full table: hardware results.

docs.title: Remote access
docs.text: By default clef binds 127.0.0.1: only the machine it runs on can call it. This page covers calling it from other machines on your local network, and what to add if you expose it further.

docs.title: Two kinds of keys
docs.text:
• Env keys (CLEF_API_KEY, CLEF_API_KEYS): full admin, no quota, the global rate limit. They are the break-glass key and the bootstrap: the first admin key is made with one of them, or with clef keys create. They are read at startup. A managed key may not share a name with an env key: the server refuses such a key (401) and logs a warning at startup; run clef keys revoke NAME or rename the env key. (The server is the authority, since the env of clef keys can differ from the server's.)
  • Managed keys (clef keys ... or the console Keys tab): a principal (a name) with scopes, an optional daily quota and rate limit, and one to five keys (clef_live_<id>_<secret>). Only the SHA-256 of a key is stored; the secret is shown once, when it is created or rotated. Changes made in the console or through /v1/admin/keys apply at once; changes made with clef keys while the server runs apply within about 10 seconds.

Auth is on when an env key exists or any managed key was ever created, and it never turns off by itself: revoking the last managed key leaves the server locked until you make a new one (clef keys create works with the server stopped, straight on the database).

clef keys create ci-bot --scope classify,jobs --quota 50000 --expires 90d   # prints the key once
clef keys create ops --scope admin                                         # an admin key for the console
clef keys list
clef keys rotate ci-bot --grace 24h     # new key now; the old ones keep working for 24 h
clef keys revoke ci-bot --key-id ab3...  # one key; without --key-id the principal is disabled for good
clef keys update ci-bot --quota none --scope classify,jobs,ops
clef keys usage ci-bot --days 30

Scopes: classify (the model routes, GET /v1/classifiers, /v1/models, /v1/evaluate), jobs (/v1/jobs*), classifiers (create / change / delete saved classifiers), ops (stats, log, events), urgent (urgent jobs) and admin (everything, plus /v1/admin/* and the Keys tab). A key without the route's scope gets 403. GET /v1/whoami shows the caller's name, scopes and quota use.

Daily quota. Counts records (a batch of 50 is 50) per UTC day. Computed records are charged; results served from the result cache are free. A job is charged in full when it is submitted, and the part it did not process comes back if it is cancelled or fails. Over the quota: 429 with Retry-After (seconds to the next UTC midnight); the OpenAI routes report insufficient_quota. Responses carry X-Quota-Limit and X-Quota-Remaining.

Audit log. Key changes, job cancel / delete and saved-classifier changes are recorded with who, what, when and IP (GET /v1/admin/audit, also in the console). Secrets are never recorded.

docs.title: LAN setup
docs.text:
1. Create a keys file (one name:key per line, # comments allowed). Generate strong keys:
mkdir -p ~/.config/clef
{
  echo "# name:key"
  echo "ci-bot:$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
  echo "laptop:$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
} > ~/.config/clef/keys
chmod 600 ~/.config/clef/keys
  1. Start the server bound to all interfaces:
CLEF_HOST=0.0.0.0 CLEF_API_KEYS=$HOME/.config/clef/keys CLEF_RATE_LIMIT=120 clef serve --detach

CLEF_API_KEYS also accepts the list inline: ci-bot:KEY1,laptop:KEY2. CLEF_API_KEY=KEY is a single key named default. These are env keys (full admin: with several of them, each can see and delete every job, edit every classifier and mint keys, and the server warns at startup); for scoped keys with quotas use clef keys create instead of, or next to, them. Binding a non-loopback host with no key (env or managed) logs a loud warning at startup; do not ignore it.

  1. Allow the port through the firewall for your LAN only (below).

  2. Call it from another machine:

curl http://192.168.1.50:8910/v1/classify -H "X-API-Key: $CLEF_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": "Checkout is down", "labels": ["billing", "technical"]}'

Authorization: Bearer <key> works too. The Python and JS clients take the key as api_key= / apiKey.

All /v1/* routes, and the Hugging Face routes (/hf/models/*), then require a key (401 otherwise, 403 for a key without the route's scope); /v1/admin/* always requires an admin key, even when auth is off; the OpenAI SDKs send it as Authorization: Bearer from their api_key setting. Open routes: /, static files, /health, /livez, /readyz, /docs, /openapi.json. The console is served without a key, but its API calls need one: enter it in the console settings. The console sends the key in the X-API-Key header, also for the live event stream. /v1/events still accepts ?key= for plain EventSource clients (they cannot set headers); this puts the key in the URL, so on untrusted networks use TLS.

docs.title: Keys and logging
docs.text:
• Each key has a name. The name (never the key) is stored on every request in /v1/log and counted in /v1/stats (by_key), so you can see who is calling.
  • Keys are compared in constant time. clef never logs them: ?key= values are written as REDACTED in the access log. If you turn on the access log of a reverse proxy, mask the key there too; see Keys in proxy logs for Caddy and nginx.
  • Rotate a managed key with clef keys rotate NAME (or the console): the old key keeps working for the grace period (default 24 h), so callers can switch without a gap. Env keys are rotated by editing the keys file and restarting clef serve (they are read at startup).

docs.title: Rate limit
docs.text: CLEF_RATE_LIMIT=N allows N inference requests per minute per key (per client IP when auth is off), sliding 60 s window. A managed key can have its own limit (--rate-limit), which applies even when CLEF_RATE_LIMIT is 0. Counted routes: /v1/systemone, /v1/batch, /v1/classify, /v1/classify/batch, /v1/score, POST /v1/classifiers/{name}[/batch], /v1/chat/completions, /hf/models/*, /v1/evaluate and POST /v1/jobs. Over the limit: 429 with Retry-After: <seconds>. 0 (default) disables it. A batch call counts as one request, so also keep CLEF_MAX_BATCH reasonable.

docs.title: Jobs, webhooks and keys
docs.text: Async jobs belong to the principal that submitted them: other non-admin keys get 404 for them and do not see them in the job list. Admin keys, including every env key, see all jobs. Jobs and classifiers created while auth was off have no owner and are admin-only to read results of, change or delete once auth is on (non-admin keys may still run such a classifier). Webhooks are off until you set CLEF_WEBHOOK_ALLOW; list only the receivers you trust (a private address needs its IP or CIDR listed explicitly) and see Jobs & webhooks and the security policy before enabling them on an exposed server. clef.db in the state directory (or your Postgres database, with CLEF_DATABASE_URL) holds your submitted inputs and the webhook secrets in clear text, so protect that directory like the keys file.

docs.title: CORS (browser callers)
docs.text:
Off by default. To let a web page on another origin call the API:

CLEF_CORS_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com,http://localhost:5173 clef serve

* is accepted, but do not combine it with an exposed server. Allowed methods GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/OPTIONS, headers *, credentials off. Never put an API key in public front-end code: anyone who loads the page can read it. Call clef from your own backend instead.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
Open TCP 8910 (or your CLEF_PORT) to your LAN subnet only, not to the world. Replace 192.168.1.0/24.

Ubuntu (ufw)

sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 8910 proto tcp

macOS: System Settings > Network > Firewall; allow incoming connections for the Python/clef process when prompted. For a subnet rule use pf.

Windows (PowerShell, as administrator)

New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "clef" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 8910 -RemoteAddress 192.168.1.0/24 -Action Allow

Windows + WSL2: the server listens inside WSL, so Windows must forward the port. With the default NAT networking use a port proxy (the WSL address changes on restart), or set networkingMode=mirrored in %USERPROFILE%\.wslconfig (Windows 11 22H2+) and then only the firewall rule is needed:

$wsl = (wsl -d Ubuntu hostname -I).Trim().Split(' ')[0]
netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=8910 connectaddress=$wsl connectport=8910

Docker: -p 8910:8910 already publishes on all interfaces; bind to a LAN address with -p 192.168.1.50:8910:8910 if you want to limit it, and still use keys.

docs.title: Beyond the LAN: TLS reverse proxy (Caddy)
docs.text:
Do not expose the plain HTTP port to the internet. Put a reverse proxy with TLS in front, keep clef bound to 127.0.0.1, and keep API keys on. Caddyfile (certificates are obtained automatically for a public hostname):

clef.example.com {
    encode zstd gzip

    # large image/video payloads: match CLEF_MAX_BODY_MB (default 64)
    request_body {
        max_size 64MB
    }

    # no `log` directive: if you add one, mask X-Api-Key and ?key= (security.md#keys-in-proxy-logs)
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8910 {
        # server-sent events (/v1/events) must not be buffered
        flush_interval -1
    }
}

Run caddy run --config Caddyfile. For a LAN-only hostname without a public domain, use tls internal inside the site block (clients must trust Caddy's local CA). Behind a proxy every request comes from 127.0.0.1, so the rate limit is per key, not per client IP: keep API keys on.

Load balancers. Point the health check at /readyz (open, no key). To take a server out of rotation before it stops, set CLEF_DRAIN_S (e.g. 5): after SIGTERM / Ctrl-C clef keeps serving that long while /readyz answers 503 draining, then shuts down; a second signal stops it at once. Pick the probe interval x failure threshold below CLEF_DRAIN_S, and keep CLEF_DRAIN_S below your supervisor's stop timeout (10 s for docker stop). With the default 0 the listening socket closes at once and the load balancer only sees refused connections.

Additional hardening if you do expose it: set a low CLEF_RATE_LIMIT, keep CLEF_ALLOW_URL_FETCH=0 (default), keep CLEF_LOG_STATE=0 (default; request contents are not stored), and restrict by IP in the proxy where possible.

docs.title: Router and Review
docs.text:
A router grows the label set of one single-label saved classifier. Texts it cannot place are kept; every 20 of them go to an LLM that proposes new labels; clef then re-classifies those texts against the proposed set and only a proposal that clef itself confirms is shown to you (or, in auto mode, published as a new classifier version). Labels are only ever added: no merge, split, rename or retire. A router holds at most 63 labels plus other.

The router is off until you give it an LLM key. Routing itself (/v1/routers/{name}/route) works without one.

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
Put the key in a .env file next to where you run clef serve, or in ~/.config/clef/env (see Configuration). A variable already set in the environment wins over both files.

echo 'GEMINI_API_KEY=your-key' >> .env                 # or: >> ~/.config/clef/env
# systemd (deploy/clef.service) reads ~/.config/clef/env as well
# docker compose: the .env file next to docker-compose.yml is passed through by the compose file

Restart the server and check with clef doctor (it says whether the LLM is on, never the key). By default clef talks to Gemini's OpenAI-compatible endpoint with gemini-3.8-flash. Any OpenAI-compatible server works:

CLEF_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1 CLEF_LLM_MODEL=llama3 CLEF_LLM_API_KEY=ollama clef serve

Privacy

Setting the key is your consent: up to CLEF_ROUTER_MAX_INPUT_CHARS (500) characters of each buffered input are sent to the LLM host. The console shows an "external LLM: host" badge on every router. Nothing is sent without a key, and the key is never logged.

docs.title: Create and use a router
docs.text:
curl -X PUT localhost:8910/v1/routers/tickets -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "seeds": {"billing": "money, invoices, refunds", "technical": "bugs and outages"},
  "domain_hint": "customer support tickets", "mode": "review"}'

curl -X POST localhost:8910/v1/routers/tickets/route -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"input": "my password reset email never arrives"}'

seeds are optional. Without them an existing single-label classifier named like the router (or classifier) supplies the labels; with neither, the router starts cold: it answers other (reason cold) without running the model, and after 20 items one bigger LLM call proposes a starter set of up to 8 labels. clef needs at least two options, so a single seed is enough to start ([seed, other]).

Every routed result has a reason:

reason meaning kept? classified confident answer no other other won yes, buffered low_confidence the top probability is below the threshold for this label count yes, buffered ambiguous the top two labels are within margin (0.15) yes, for a human only cold the router has no labels yet yes, buffered

The threshold rises with the number of options (other included): 0.5 up to 10, 0.7 up to 30, 0.85 up to 64. Override it per router with gate.thresholds ([[10, 0.5], [30, 0.7], [64, 0.85]]) and gate.margin. These are defaults chosen for the label counts; tune them on your own data with the Evaluate screen's coverage curve.

docs.title: Proposals and the re-check
docs.text: A call happens when CLEF_ROUTER_BATCH (20) items are buffered, when the oldest has waited CLEF_ROUTER_FLUSH_S (600 s; at least 2 items, 5 for a cold start), or on POST /v1/routers/{name}/propose. The LLM is shown the current labels (to avoid duplicates) and the numbered texts; it asks for at most 3 new labels. Then clef re-classifies each proposal's member texts under current labels + the proposal + other. A proposal passes when at least half of its members (and at least 2) land on the new label, and it fails as a duplicate when most land on one existing label. Texts a person already labelled with an existing label count against the proposal. Failed proposals are kept as failed rows so you can see why. Items that no proposal takes are checked at most twice more, then become permanent_other, and their text is dropped at that moment.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
• review (default): confirmed proposals appear in the Review screen. Approve publishes them (all, or an edited subset with your own descriptions) as a new classifier version; Reject returns the texts to the buffer.
  • auto: a confirmed proposal is published at once, at most CLEF_ROUTER_MAX_NEW_PER_DAY (10) new labels per UTC day; beyond that it waits in the queue. The starter set of a cold router is exempt from that limit.

After a label set is published, the buffered texts are re-classified; those that now pass the gate are resolved by the router. Every label set is a router version (GET /v1/routers/{name}/versions); Roll back publishes an earlier one again as a new classifier version.

docs.title: The Review queue
docs.text:
One table holds router proposals and low-confidence items. Items come from routers, and from any saved classifier with a review_threshold (single-label, 0..1): interactive runs (POST /v1/classifiers/{name}[/batch], not jobs) whose confidence is below it are queued, in the classifier owner's queue. Only runs by the owner or an admin are captured (with auth off, every run): when another key runs your classifier, its inputs are never stored for review, so its text does not reach you. Media inputs are never captured.

Labelling an item re-classifies its text under the active labels before the text is purged and records whether clef agrees (prediction.recheck); the label also counts against later proposals that would absorb the same text. Input text is stored only in review rows: it is dropped when the item is resolved and after CLEF_REVIEW_TTL_DAYS (30) for rows nobody resolved (they become expired). Resolved rows keep the label, the input's sha256 and the prediction.

The Review screen of the console lists the queue (filters: kind, state, router, classifier), has a label picker and Discard for items, approve / edit / reject for proposals, and per router: its label set, versions with roll back, mode, buffer size, the LLM badge and today's calls and tokens. It needs the classifiers scope.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Route Scope PUT\|GET\|DELETE /v1/routers/{name}, GET /v1/routers, POST .../propose, GET .../versions, POST .../versions/{v}/activate classifiers POST /v1/routers/{name}/route, .../route/batch classify GET /v1/review, GET /v1/review/{id}, POST /v1/review/{id}/resolve classifiers

Routers and review rows belong to the key that created them; admins see all. resolve takes {"action": "label", "label"} or {"action": "discard"} for items, {"action": "approve", "labels"?} or {"action": "reject"} for proposals. Errors: 400 bad name, label or cap; 403 scope or owner; 404; 409 a call in flight, the classifier belongs to another router, or the row is already resolved; 502 the LLM call failed; 503 the LLM is off. Full request and response shapes: Architecture and /docs.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Please report privately through GitHub: Security tab > "Report a vulnerability" (https://github.com/MiguelCarrascoB/clef/security/advisories/new). Do not open a public issue for security problems. Include the version (clef version), the backend, and steps to reproduce. You can expect an acknowledgement within a few days; this is a one-maintainer project, so there is no formal SLA.

Supported version: the latest release (3.1.x).

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
clef runs a model on your own hardware and exposes an HTTP API. It is designed for a single trusted operator and, at most, trusted callers on a local network.

  • Local by default. CLEF_HOST defaults to 127.0.0.1. Binding any other address without API keys logs a loud warning at startup.
  • API keys. Two kinds protect every /v1/* route and the Hugging Face compatibility routes (/hf/models/*). Env keys (CLEF_API_KEY or CLEF_API_KEYS, named, from a list or a file) are full admin with no quota: treat them as break-glass credentials, and note that every env-key holder sees every job and may change every saved classifier, so env keys are not isolated from each other. A managed key whose name equals an env key's is refused (401, startup warning), so it cannot inherit that env key's ownership; the server is the authority on this, since the env seen by clef keys can differ. Managed keys (clef keys create, the console or /v1/admin/keys) belong to a principal with scopes (classify, jobs, classifiers, ops, admin, urgent; a missing scope is 403), an optional daily record quota and rate limit, expiry and revocation. A managed key is clef_live_<id>_<secret>; only its SHA-256 is stored, so it cannot be recovered, and the secret is shown once (create / rotate). A rotated principal keeps up to five keys; the old ones expire after a grace period (default 24 h). Daily quotas are counted in the memory of the one server process; they rely on the one-server-per-database rule (a Postgres advisory lock refuses a second server), so do not run two servers on one database. Auth is on when an env key exists or any managed key ever existed, and never turns off by itself (revoking the last managed key does not open the server). /v1/admin/* always needs an admin key, even when auth is off. clef keys works directly on the database (that is how the first admin key is made, with the server stopped, as the OS user who can read the state directory), so access to the state directory is access to key management; protect it like the keys file. The OpenAI-compatible routes read the same keys as Authorization: Bearer, so the official SDKs work unchanged. Keys are compared in constant time (managed keys by their hash), and only the principal name is recorded in the request log and stats. Key changes are audited (who, what, when, IP; never a secret). Keep the keys file out of version control and readable only by you (chmod 600). The SSE endpoint /v1/events also accepts ?key= for plain EventSource clients, which puts the key in the URL; do not use it across untrusted networks without TLS. The console sends the X-API-Key header instead.
  • Rate limit and quota. CLEF_RATE_LIMIT limits inference requests per minute per key (per IP when auth is off) and returns 429 with Retry-After; a managed key can have its own limit. A managed key can also have a daily quota of records per UTC day (computed records only; cache hits are free; a job is charged at submit and refunded for what it did not process), refused with 429 and Retry-After. It is a safety net against accidents and noisy clients, not a DDoS defence.
  • Rate limit scope. Besides the classification routes, POST /v1/chat/completions, POST /hf/models/*, POST /v1/evaluate and POST /v1/jobs count against the limit. POST /v1/evaluate/metrics runs no inference and is not counted.
  • CORS is off unless CLEF_CORS_ORIGINS is set. Do not embed API keys in browser code.
  • SSRF guard. Fetching media from http(s) URLs is off by default (CLEF_ALLOW_URL_FETCH=0). When enabled, hosts are resolved and any non-global address (private, loopback, link-local, multicast) is refused, redirects are not followed, and downloads are size-capped (CLEF_URL_FETCH_MAX_MB) with a total timeout. Data URLs are the default way to send media.
  • Input limits. Body size, token count, images, videos, pixels, frames, labels, questions and batch size are all capped and validated (CLEF_MAX_*). Evaluation and jobs add their own caps: CLEF_MAX_EVAL_ROWS (500 rows per /v1/evaluate call), CLEF_MAX_JOB_EVAL_ROWS (100000), CLEF_MAX_JOB_ITEMS (100000 items per job), CLEF_MAX_JOBS (100 queued or running jobs, then 409) and a 16 KB limit on job metadata. Errors are generic 500s with a request id; tracebacks stay in the server log.
  • Webhooks and SSRF. A webhook makes the server send a request to an address chosen by the API caller, so the feature is off until the operator sets CLEF_WEBHOOK_ALLOW (hosts, *.suffix patterns, IPs or CIDRs). The list is checked when the job is submitted and again on every delivery attempt: the hostname is resolved at that moment, every returned address must be public or inside a listed IP / CIDR, and the connection is pinned to the checked address, so a DNS answer that changes later (rebinding) is refused. Link-local (cloud metadata), multicast, unspecified and reserved addresses are refused even when a CIDR covers them. IPv6 addresses that embed an IPv4 address (NAT64 64:ff9b::/96 and 64:ff9b:1::/48, 6to4, Teredo) are judged by that IPv4 address, and site-local IPv6 is refused, so a translated address cannot reach a private host. Redirects are never followed, environment proxies are ignored, credentials in the URL are rejected and API keys are never sent. Deliveries are signed (X-Clef-Signature, HMAC-SHA256 over "<timestamp>.<body>"); receivers should verify it and check the timestamp. Use https for anything that leaves your machine. The TLS path has not been tested against a real TLS server yet. POST /v1/jobs/{id}/webhook/redeliver resends a failed delivery only to the job's stored URL, needs the owner's key, is rate limited and re-runs every check above. Details: docs/jobs.md.
  • Jobs: ownership, retention, disk. With keys configured, a job belongs to the principal that submitted it; other non-admin keys get 404 and do not see it in the list. Admin keys (all env keys included) see every job. This is a convenience between cooperating callers, not tenant isolation, and jobs or classifiers created while auth was off (no owner) become admin-only once auth is on: non-admin keys get 404 for such a job, 403 when changing or deleting such a classifier, and may still run it. Jobs are stored in the database (clef.db in the state directory, or CLEF_DATABASE_URL): the submitted payload of every job (your input texts), its result rows and webhook secrets are stored in clear text (HMAC needs the secret; evaluate rows also keep the input and gold label). Finished jobs are deleted CLEF_JOB_TTL_HOURS after they finish (default 168; 0 keeps them forever) or on DELETE /v1/jobs/{id}. Protect the state directory like the API keys file, and delete clef.db (with the server stopped) to drop everything.
  • Database files and URLs. A new clef.db is created readable by its owner only (0600 on POSIX), and so are the copies clef backup writes to <state dir>/backups/; a clef.db copied from a v3.1 jobs.db is 0600 too, but the original kept as jobs.db.migrated keeps its old permissions (delete it once you are happy). With Postgres, everyone who can read that database reads the same payloads and secrets: give clef its own database and role, and use TLS (?sslmode=require) to a remote server. CLEF_DATABASE_URL carries the password: clef never logs it, and /health, clef doctor and the clef db commands show it as ***. Prefer a systemd EnvironmentFile or a compose .env with tight permissions over the command line. The audit log (audit_log: saved-classifier changes, key changes, job cancel / delete; GET /v1/admin/audit) records who, what and when, never a secret or request content; it has no purge. Job results exported as CSV neutralise cells that start with =, +, - or @, so opening them in a spreadsheet does not run formulas.
  • No secrets in logs. Request state (the text you classify) is not logged unless CLEF_LOG_STATE=1, but jobs do store it on disk (see above). clef's own logs never contain a key: headers are not logged, and the values of the key, api_key and token query parameters are replaced with REDACTED in the uvicorn access log (also with CLEF_LOG_FORMAT=json). A reverse proxy in front of clef keeps its own logs; see Keys in proxy logs. Saved classifier names are validated and never used to build paths from raw input.
  • Console and vendored code. The console is a zero-build app served by the server with no runtime CDN calls. Its three vendored libraries (Preact, htm, uPlot) and their licences are listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.
  • Model and dependencies. Weights come from the pinned Hugging Face revision; CLEF_MODEL_PATH should point only at files you trust (the model code in the release directory is imported and executed). Dependencies are pinned in requirements/.

Out of scope / not provided: TLS (use a reverse proxy, see docs/remote-access.md), per-user authorization beyond the scopes above (all keys that may run the model have the same access to it; job and saved classifier ownership only scope visibility and changes), multi-tenant isolation, protection against a malicious model directory.

docs.title: Keys in proxy logs
docs.text:
clef masks keys in its own logs, but a reverse proxy writes its own access log. Keep the key out of it too: drop the X-API-Key and Authorization headers and mask (or drop) the query string.

Caddy logs every request header when a log directive is on, and redacts only Authorization, Cookie and Proxy-Authorization by default, so X-Api-Key would be written in clear text:

clef.example.com {
    log {
        format filter {
            request>uri query {
                replace key REDACTED
                replace api_key REDACTED
                replace token REDACTED
            }
            request>headers>X-Api-Key delete
        }
    }
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8910
}

nginx logs no request headers by default (do not add $http_x_api_key or $http_authorization to a log_format), but the default combined format logs $request, which includes the query. Log $uri (the path without the query) instead:

log_format clef '$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request_method $uri $server_protocol" '
                '$status $body_bytes_sent "$http_referer" "$http_user_agent"';
access_log /var/log/nginx/clef.access.log clef;

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Run clef doctor first (clef doctor --json for a bug report). On Windows + WSL use .\clef.ps1 doctor.

Contents: CUDA - ROCm under WSL2 - MPS (macOS) - CPU - Common

docs.title: CUDA
docs.text:
Untested on hardware at the time of writing; these are the known failure modes of the stack.

  • CUDA not available / backend falls to cpu: the installed torch is a CPU build, or the driver is missing. Check nvidia-smi, then python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())". Reinstall from requirements/cuda.txt.
  • Driver / toolkit mismatch (CUDA driver version is insufficient, no kernel image is available): the driver must support the CUDA version of the torch wheel (nvidia-smi shows the maximum supported CUDA version at the top right). Update the driver; you do not need a system CUDA toolkit for the wheels.
  • "The fast path is not available" warning (transformers): flash-linear-attention and causal-conv1d are missing. The model still runs through a slower torch fallback. Install flash-linear-attention (part of the CUDA lock file) and causal-conv1d; clef doctor shows which one is missing.
  • causal-conv1d fails to build: it compiles CUDA code and needs nvcc matching the torch CUDA version, a C++ compiler and ninja. Prefer a prebuilt wheel matching your torch/CUDA/Python, or install the CUDA toolkit of the same major.minor as torch.version.cuda. If it cannot be built, run without it; correctness is unchanged. Built from source on WSL2 + Ubuntu 24.04 with cuda-toolkit-12-8 (do not install the cuda or cuda-drivers metapackages inside WSL), uv pip install ninja setuptools wheel, then CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-12.8 TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=8.9 MAX_JOBS=6 uv pip install causal-conv1d --no-build-isolation (set the arch list to your card; it took about 23 minutes). On an RTX 4070 Ti it did not change speed measurably (p50 170.3 to 167.5 ms), so skipping it costs little there.
  • CLEF_QUANT errors: on CUDA int8 and nf4 use bitsandbytes (pip install bitsandbytes, part of the cuda extra); if it cannot find the CUDA libraries, check python -m bitsandbytes. CLEF_QUANT_BACKEND=torchao needs pip install "clef-local[quant]". nf4 exists only in bitsandbytes. Quantized probabilities differ slightly from bf16 (numbers on CUDA are pending hardware; on ROCm see Smaller GPUs).
  • Out of memory on load or under load: bf16 needs ~19.5 GB peak. Close other GPU users, use a 24 GB card, or lower the footprint: CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB=<N-1> (lossless) or CLEF_QUANT=int8; the Smaller GPUs table says what fits where. Preflight (CLEF_PREFLIGHT=1) reports this before loading and clef doctor prints a recommendation. At runtime an OOM returns 503 and the server keeps running; lower CLEF_MAX_MICROBATCH or CLEF_MAX_TOKENS, or raise the cap.
  • bf16 on older GPUs (pre-Ampere): bf16 is not supported; clef falls back to fp16 with a warning. Check parity with bench/parity.py.

docs.title: ROCm under WSL2
docs.text:
This is the verified setup (RX 7900 XTX, ROCm 7.2).

  • No CUDA GPUs are available / torch sees no device: HSA_ENABLE_DXG_DETECTION=1 must be set (clef sets it automatically when /dev/dxg exists; required until ROCm 7.13+ in WSL). If you run torch yourself, export it.
  • /dev/dxg missing: update the Windows AMD Adrenalin driver, make sure WSL2 (not WSL1) is used (wsl -l -v), then wsl --shutdown.
  • Permission denied on /dev/dxg or /dev/kfd: add your user to the render group (sudo usermod -aG render $USER), then restart the distro.
  • WSL stops the server a few seconds after you close the terminal: WSL shuts an idle distro down ~15 s after the last wsl.exe session exits. clef.ps1 start keeps a hidden keep-alive session for this reason; use it (or the systemd user service with systemd=true in /etc/wsl.conf, see deploy/wsl.conf.sample) instead of a bare wsl -e clef serve --detach.
  • MSYS path conversion (Git Bash): wsl ... /mnt/c/... arguments get rewritten to C:/Program Files/Git/.... Prefix the command with MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1, or use PowerShell.
  • expandable_segments is not supported on ROCm/WSL: do not set PYTORCH_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True (it logs a warning and is ignored at best).
  • First forwards take seconds to minutes: one-time Triton/SDPA kernel compilation per input shape. The startup warmup covers the length buckets; caches live in ~/.triton/cache. The first warmup after a fresh install takes ~110 s, later ones ~12 s.
  • Out of memory in WSL: set memory=26GB in %USERPROFILE%\.wslconfig (for a 32 GB host); it applies after wsl --shutdown.
  • causal-conv1d: its HIP build does not work on WSL-ROCm yet. flash-linear-attention is active and the torch fallback for the convolution is already fast; the fast-path warning is expected for causal_conv1d only.
  • bench refuses to run: the server holds ~19.6 GB of VRAM; stop it first (clef stop) or pass --force.
  • AMD telemetry under WSL is partial: measured on the RX 7900 XTX (ROCm 7.2), amdsmi reports GPU utilization and temperature, but no power, and its VRAM usage is nonsense (clef drops it and charts the allocator figure instead). rocm-smi is not tried under WSL. Without the amdsmi Python package, telemetry shows "unavailable"; that is harmless.

docs.title: MPS (macOS)
docs.text:
Untested on hardware at the time of writing.

  • bf16 on macOS < 14: MPS bf16 needs macOS 14+. clef falls back to fp16 with a warning; update macOS or check parity with bench/parity.py.
  • Memory pressure / the Mac becomes unresponsive: the model takes ~19.5 GB of unified memory; 32 GB is the realistic floor. Close other apps, lower CLEF_MAX_MICROBATCH, keep images small (CLEF_MAX_PIXELS). Preflight warns when free memory looks too low.
  • NotImplementedError: ... not currently implemented for the MPS device: clef sets PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1 automatically so unsupported ops run on the CPU. If you import torch yourself before clef, export it in your shell.
  • fla Triton kernels not available: expected. Triton does not run on macOS, so the torch fallback is used and the transformers fast-path warning is normal.
  • CLEF_QUANT=nf4 is refused: nf4 needs bitsandbytes (NVIDIA or AMD). CLEF_QUANT=int8 works through torchao (pip install torchao, already in the mps extra) but is not validated on Apple Silicon.
  • CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu does nothing: a Mac shares one memory pool between device and host, so offload has no effect there (a warning is logged). Use CLEF_QUANT=int8 instead.
  • Slow first request: MPS compiles kernels lazily; the startup warmup covers the common shapes.
  • Closing the lid / sleep stops the server: use the launchd agent in deploy/ and keep the Mac awake (caffeinate -i).

docs.title: CPU
docs.text:
• CLEF_OFFLOAD has no effect: the CPU backend already runs from host RAM.
  • Out of memory / the machine swaps: the model needs ~40 GB of RAM on CPU (weights plus activations). Use a GPU backend if you have one.
  • Very slow: expected, seconds per record. CPU mode is for development and CI (the unit tests never load the model). Set CLEF_WARMUP=0 to skip the warmup.
  • Backend detected as cpu on a machine with a GPU: you installed a CPU torch build. Reinstall from the matching lock file, or force a device with CLEF_DEVICE=cuda|rocm|mps to get an explicit error with a hint.

docs.title: Smaller-memory modes
docs.text:
See Smaller GPUs for the numbers.

  • Load fails with a "not enough memory" message under CLEF_OFFLOAD=cpu: even streaming every layer does not fit under CLEF_MAX_DEVICE_MEMORY_GB. Raise the cap (the smallest one measured to work is 7 GB; 6 crashed while loading on WSL2 because too many layers had to be pinned) or add CLEF_QUANT=int8.
  • Host RAM or WSL2 memory: offload keeps what it moved off the GPU in pinned host memory (~6 GB at a 15 GB cap, ~15 GB at 7 GB). On WSL2 raise memory= in .wslconfig. Loading briefly uses more (memory-mapped weight files).
  • A very long input returns 503 GpuOutOfMemory with offload: activations exceeded the 2.5 GB reserve. Lower CLEF_MAX_MICROBATCH, shorten the input or raise the cap. The server stays up.
  • Slower than bf16: expected. The layers kept on the host are copied over PCIe each forward (p50 +15% at a 15 GB cap, 3.6x at 7 GB).

docs.title: Jobs, webhooks and compatibility routes
docs.text:
• 400 webhook.url: ... on submit: webhooks are off until the operator sets CLEF_WEBHOOK_ALLOW; the host (or IP / CIDR for a private address) must be listed. Link-local, multicast and reserved addresses are always refused.
  • A webhook never arrives: check webhook.deliveries in GET /v1/jobs/{id} (last_status, last_error). The allow-list is re-checked, and the host re-resolved, on every attempt. Retries stop after CLEF_WEBHOOK_ATTEMPTS.
  • 404 for a job you submitted: another API key. Jobs are visible only to the key that created them (and to keys with the admin scope); a key without the jobs scope gets 403.
  • 409 on POST /v1/jobs: CLEF_MAX_JOBS queued or running jobs; retry after Retry-After. On cancel / delete it means the job is already finished / still active.
  • A job stays queued: look at waiting_reason in GET /v1/jobs/{id}: off_hours (its window opens at next_window_at; urgent skips it), active_limit (CLEF_JOB_ACTIVE jobs are already running) or empty (it is about to be admitted). A job that stays running without progress and says off_hours or turn is waiting for its window or for other jobs' chunks. While the model is loading a job waits instead of failing.
  • 400 missing_schema from /v1/chat/completions: clef decides, it does not generate text. Send a response_format JSON schema (or one forced tool); see compatibility.
  • huggingface_hub cannot find the model: pass the full route, model="http://127.0.0.1:8910/hf/models/clef-flash", instead of setting HF_ENDPOINT.
  • POST /v1/evaluate rejects the rows: more than CLEF_MAX_EVAL_ROWS (500), or a gold label that is not in the label set. Large sets: submit an evaluate job.

docs.title: Common
docs.text:
• Port already in use: something else answers on 8910. clef status shows whether it is clef. Stop it (clef stop), or use CLEF_PORT=8911 / clef serve --port 8911. clef serve --detach refuses to start when the port answers.
  • 401 Unauthorized: keys are configured; send X-API-Key: <key> or Authorization: Bearer <key>. Check the key name in the keys file (name:key). See remote-access.md.
  • 429 Too Many Requests: CLEF_RATE_LIMIT is exceeded for that key; wait Retry-After seconds or raise the limit.
  • 503 Service Unavailable: the model is still loading/warming (clef status, /health) or the device ran out of memory. The clients retry with backoff.
  • Model not found: run clef download. Path resolution: CLEF_MODEL_PATH if set, else ~/models/clef-flash if it holds a release, else the pinned snapshot in the Hugging Face cache. The server never downloads on its own (/health shows status: error with the message).
  • Download fails or stalls: clef download is resumable, just run it again. It needs ~21 GB free; behind a proxy set HTTPS_PROXY. Set HF_HOME to put the cache on another disk.
  • Not enough disk space: the weights are ~19 GB; clef doctor and clef download check this up front.
  • Where are the logs / state? clef logs -f. The state directory is ~/.local/state/clef on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/clef on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA%\clef on Windows (CLEF_STATE_DIR overrides; CLEF_LOG_DIR is a legacy alias). It holds server.log, server.pid and clef.db (jobs and saved classifiers; after an upgrade from v3.1 also jobs.db.migrated and classifiers.imported/, which you can delete).
  • Upgrading from v2: see the migration notes in the CHANGELOG.
